anese policemen and several

NORTH ALLERTON, Eng, Mar.
"A riot involving 70 British Army
prisoners was put down by troops
last night after the rioters set fire
to North Allerton Military Prison
and wrecked its interior.


The last seven rioters were cap
tured after they had held out on a
roof top for more than eight hours,
pelting the troops below with slate
shingles and other missiles. Five
members of the prison guard were
injured, none seriously.


Firemen quelled the blaze in the
building after four-hour fight and
then turned their hoses on the
rioters, causing all but the last
seven holdouts to surrender. The
prisoners, most of them recently
transferred from the British Army
on the Rhine, were protesting the
food and no-smoking rule.

District boxing fans. steamed up

Washington is a better man than

1910 for Perry It's a question of

Maybe the fight would not draw

tracks were blown up at three places
along the LYDIA -Haifa line early
today in the vicinity of the Ras Ell
Ain railway station, which had been
destroyed by bombs IL hours pre-
viously.

the Jaffa-Tel Aviv railway line last
night. No casualties were reported.


Police sought three Jews whom
they accused of placing the bombs
which destroyed the Ras Ell Ain sta
ton, killed one Arab and injured
three British sappers who were try
ing to remove the explosive charges.


Authorities pointed out the SINH
larity between yesterdays incident
and the method employed by the
Jewish underground organization
Irgun Zvai Leumi, when a Jerusa-
lem station was destroyed last week
Four days ago the group said it
would continue to attack railway
installations.


Oficials also reported the death
of fourth British policeman, in
jured in Fridays BOBBY trap explo-
sion during a raid on a suspected
arms cache in the Bukharian area
of Jerusalem.

The results of the elections held
last Friday for the Lower House of
the Dutch Parliament, collectively
termed the States General, conform
closely to the pattern set in recent
elections held both in neighboring
Belgium and, to a somewhat lesser
extent, in France. The outstanding
feature is the strength shown by the
Christian conservatives. Almost
equally significant are: The increase
of the Communists. the recession of
the moderate Socialists and the vir-
tual eclipse of the old-fashioned
Liberals.


Although the Netherlands are his
torically a Protestant country, ap-
proXimately one-third of the popu-
lation are Roman Catholics, concen-
trated especially in the southern
provinces, which were acquired from
the Spanish Netherlands (now Bel
gium) during the Dutch wars of lib
Grafton. The inhabitants of the
original Seven Provinces" of the
north which revolted from Spanish
rule have remained strongly Protes-
tant, except in the big cities, which
contain not only Roman Catholic
migrants from the south but also
an extremely radical development
among the industrial workers, today
frankly Communist in character.


The Roman Catholics have long
been we'll organized political
party, numerically the strongest in
the last preWar Parliament elected
in 1887. The provisional regime in
stalled after Dutch liberation from
the Axis was predominantly leftist
in complexion and was headed by
Premier Willem Schermerhorn, rep
resenting the Labor party, CORE
spending closely to the British Labor
party, with a platform of moderate
Socialism.


This arrangement has now been
upset by the elections, which re-
tul lieu JILL Gy - GWO SdlllOllCo dS
against the Labor party's twenty
nine. Premier Schermerhorn has
accordingly handed in his resigna-
tion to Queen Wilhelmina. How
ever, the precise makeup of the new
cabinet is not yet certain, due to the
fact that several other political par
ties are we'll represented. The Prot
estant bloc, which is essentially con-
servative, won twenty-three seats,
while the Liberals trailed with only
six. The Communists made a very
strong showing in the big cities,
polling 100000 votes and winning
ten seats in the Lower House The
Dutch Communists are showing
militant spirit, threatening among
other things to call a dock strike

The Navy is sending its three new
and mighty battle cruisers to the
limbo of laid-up ships.


Their chances of emerging for ac-
tive duty are slim, Navy men said
today.


The 27,500-ton ships-the Alaska,
Guam and Hawaii-were built to
match the punching power of COM
parable enemy vessels, such as Ger
many's Scharnhorst.


But the changing mode of war
fare and manpower limitations has
headed them for obscure anchorages
long before the time when fighting
ships usually become obsolete. With
emphasis on air-sea battle, the Navy
decided the need for men to man
the carriers of the postwar fleet was
greater than for crews to keep the
battleships in commission.


The Alaska was commissioned in
June, 1914; the Guam in September
OF the same year. The Hawaii was
scheduled for completion this year.
The original program for the Alaska
class ships called for six vessels, but
contracts for three were Cancelled in
June, 1943.

This polyglot port on Africa's
northwest tip, not far from Britain's
Gibraltar and the strategic Mediter-
ranean, is small-scale testing ground
of postwar international cooperation.


Eight nations now work together in
the provisional government of a 145-
square-mile International zone inhab-
tied by some 100000 Moslem Moors,
Moroccan Jews, Spanish, French, Eng
ish, Portuguese, Italians and other
nationals.


Soviet Russia, which has asked in the
UNO for Mediterranean trusteeships,
is question mark. The Russians took
part In the Paris conference las> August
that set up the provisional government
and are entitled to consulate here and
seats on the International Committee
Of Control and Legislative Assembly.
But they haven't shown up yet and
some have been betting that they
would not. Yet the big obstacle to Rus
sian participation, Franco Spain, is on
the way out of Tangier.


Tangier was international before the
war. Spain occupied it while other ma
tions were busy with war, in June 1910,
with the announced policy of protect
ing its neutrality" and took full charge.
The Paris conference-of United States,
British, French and Russian experts
admitted the Spanish to the provi-
sional government but, partly because of
Russian insistence, barred them from
discussions of permanent interna-
tional zone setup as long as Franco
stayed in power. These discussions are
scheduled for April-again in Paris.


In the provisional legislative assembly
France and Spain have four members
each, Britain and Italy three each and
the United States, Belgium, the Neither
lands and Portugal one each. Consuls
OF these nations make up the control
committee. Cuba, Norway, Sweden and
Switzerland also have Tangier consuls.


On occasion. United States spokesmen
have said-though they won't be quoted
now-that they will approve nothing
short of a real international govern
ment here. Some highly vocal Tangier
groups charge the current control is not
so much international as French.

SAIGON, Indo-China, April g.
A giant French ammunition
dump on the northern outskirts
of Saigon exploded this morning
and two hours later a shattering
series of explosions continued to
rock the city.


The French Army threw barri-
cades around the danger zone and
began the evacuation of all civilians


Truckloads of wounded, includ-
ing women, children and French
servicemen, were still streaming into
the hospitals at noon.


More than so wounded persons
officially were reported admitted to
hospitals in the half hour following
the first blast at 1890 am. Hospital
officials said they lost count after
that.


Communications Disrupted.


Henri Cedille, commissioner for
Cochin China, issued a special COM
munique saying that the explosion
was due to an accident and re-
quested the public to remain calm


Normal press communications
from the city were disrupted, since
the Saigon radio station was in
the explosion zone. The British
Army Signal Corps was furnishing
an emergency press service.


The sky was clouded with black
smoke and the smell OF gunpowder
pervaded the city.


Public Near Panic.


Refugees from within the ex-
ploSion area said that scores of
houses had been demolished by the
repeated blasts. The public was in
a state Of near panic and roads
were crowded with refugees leaving
town.


Windows and glassware were shat
tered for miles around the explo-
sion sector. Rue Catinat, the lead
ing shopping district, was Uttered
with rubble and glass fragments.
Military authorities refused every
one admittance to the northern part
of the section and said that a
number of 1900 pound bombs stored
in the dump still had not exploded.

~ Palestine drab and

gateway to the promised land for

Survivors of Nazi pogroms and
Europe's concentration camps, they
have brayed great obstacles on a
long and hazardous road. only to
wind up once more behind barbed
wire and guns.


But the camp is the last mile
stone of the journey Here they will
receive the certificates which will
admit them to Palestine to live as
legal residents. The process usually
takes about two weeks-two weeks
of virtual Imprisonment, but the
certainty Of release makes that an
almost minor detail The momen-
tary shadow that crosses their faces
is only reflex memory Of incredible
past experiences.


After kissing the ground of their
long-lost Israel, after the wild JOY
of arrival, after the relief of debark
ing from cramped, foul smelling
little ships, they pass through heavy
gates again, shut away for time
from their goal But they &C
through singing and their wobbly
sea legs carry them willingly.


This is the way more than 5000
Jews have been introduced to Pal
estine since last December. Frank
Noel, Associated Press photographer
and | came in with a group Of 500

illegal immigrants are charged
against the official quota of 1900
month. but these are drawn upon
for weeks in advance which, In
effect, raises the actual monthly
admissions above the legal max
imum. Immigrants in June, for
instance, might be charged TO the
August quota. Efforts to arrange

displaced Jews in Europe, as pro-
vided in the recent Anglo
report, would lift the official quotas
and balance" the books

the clearing station, The well-organ-

efficiency. The government supplies
the food. The Jewish agency sup
plies doctors and volunteer medical
helpers and STATS the kitchens
They work together to index these
people and distribute them to places
where they are most likely to sue
ceed in their new existence.

guards and the loaded guns?

the officials explain In the first

/ These must not be allowed TO

Once there were a little boy and
girl named Andy and Caro-, They
lived one mile away from the woods.
They each had 8 pony.


One day, they took their lunch
and got on their ponies and rode to
the woods. Andy started climbing a
tree to get some leaves for scrap
book. He saw a robins nest in the
tree. A mother robin was sitting on
some eggs, waiting for them to
hatch into baby birds.


Andy quickly got down from the
tree so he wouldn't disturb the
mother bird. He thought that some
time he would come back, after the
birds had left, and get the nest to
show his mother He saw the father
bird bringing a worm to the mother,
because If she went for her own
food, the eggs would get cold and
the baby birds would not hatch.


Andy looked around for Carol.
There she was, picking some wild
flowers. There were purple and
orange ones. Carol put her flowers
in a basket and then they had
lunch. After they had eaten, they
went home.

territory.

of fractions to 2 points or more were

Although at this writing the re-
turns are not complete, it is clear
that the people of Greece have
voted overwhelmingly for the return
of King George II of the Hellenes
to the Greek throne.


This outcome had been predicted
by the heads of the present Royalist-
minded Greek government which
brought about the plebiscite. 1t had
likewise been conceded by the oppo-
sition elements. But the reasons for
these concurrent prophecies were
very different. The RoyaliStS con-
tended that the great majority of
the Greek people would vote for the
Kings return if they had the chance
to vote on the matter. The opposi-
ton elements, especially the Com
munists, charged that the plebiscite
would be rigged by the government
and that the outcome would be
delusive and meaningless.


How do the facts bear out those
contentious? Thus far the evidence
seems to point clearly to the basic
honesty with which the referendum
was held. Dispatches from Ameri-
can correspondents on the spot, who
moved about freely, describe normal
voting procedures, with no official
pressure and relatively little dis
order. At least one of these cor
respondents, A. C. SedgWick of the
New York Times. was in Greece at
the time of the previous plebiscite
on the same issue, eleven years ago,
and stresses the difference; because
in 1885 the dictatorial regime of
General Kondylis acted with pal
pable fraud and duress, turning in
q result favoring the Kings restora-
ton by nearly 100 per cent.


Nothing like this has happened
today. The plebiscite results, while
giving the King a substantial over
all majority, reflect in their details
what has long been known of the
political lines which divide the
Greek people. King George swept
the PeloponnesuS overwhelmingly
but that southernmost peninsula of
the mainland has always been
Royalist stronghold At the other
extreme is the island of Crete,
an equally traditional Republican
stronghold, where the King was
showed under. In Athens and other
large cities the vote went along
class lines, Communist strength
showing in the workingmen's quar-
terS.


incidentally it should be noted
that the opposition was both Repub-
lican and Communist. Provision
was made for expressing this diver
sity by handing the voters three
slips of paper-one bearing the
Kings name, another the Greek
word Demokratih, which means Re
public" and the third blank, though

HOUSTON, Tex, Nov. 30.-An
explosion and fire at the Eastern
States oil refinery on the Houston
ship channel engulfed eight raw
gasoline storage tanks today and
injured a reported eight persons.


More than 100 firemen battled
to keep the raging blaze from
spreading to other sections of the
plant, which is at the edge of the
city.


Seven Houston firemen and one
refinery employe were reported
burned. Three were hospitalized.


According to refinery employees,
the fire started from undetermined
cause in a 1000 barrel storage tank.
While firemen were battling this
blaze the tank blew up and its top
was blown onto another of the nine
tanks grouped in the area. Blazing
gasoline was thrown over the others,
and eight burst or exploded inter-
mitently.
headline:
Houston Fire Blows Up
Eight Gasoline Tanks

Among the worlds peoples, none
has had more consistently tragic
history than the Armenians. The
Armenian homeland is the belt of
high plateau. ribbed by still loftier
mountains and cleft by valleys,
which extends from Eastern Asia
Minor to Western Persia and the
southern portion of what is now
termed Transcaucasia But the Ar
menian folk have spread broadly
from this central nucleus, especially
through Asia Minor. their chief off,
shoot being in the Taurus Noun
tains overlooking the Mediterranean,
where they long maintained a semi
independent state known as Lesser
Armenia.


The root of Armenias troubles lies
in the geographic fact that the long
valleys, running east and west, form
natural highways for invaders from
either direction. and that those
highways have for ages been main
roads for migrating peoples. Never
numerous or strong enough to de-
fend their country from invasion,
the Armenians possess true ma
tional consciousness and intense
racial solidarity which has enabled
them to retain their identity through
the most prolonged periods of sub
lection to alien rule.


Armenia was one of the first lands
to be Christianized, it's conversion
preceding by nearly a century that
of the Roman Empire. However, the
Armenian Church was doctrinally
distinct from that adopted by the
Roman world, and this has empha-
sized the distinctiveness of Armenia
and it's people. Regarded as schis-
MATES by Roman Catholics and
Greek Orthodox alike. the Arme-
mans have nevertheless been per-
secuted by the Moslems for their
Christianity. to which they remain
invincibly attached as part of their
national as we'll as their spiritual
heritage.


Down to World War One, the bulk
of the Armenian people were within
the political boundaries of Turkey,
though considerable sections dwelt
in Russian Transcaucasia and Per-
STA. The Turkish Armenians were,
however. almost destroyed by the
terrible massacres and deportations
during that war, while the survivors
either took refuge with their kindred
across the Russian border or scat
tered broadcast over the Near and
Middle East. where they formed
colonies in Egypt, Syria and other

text:
The proposal presented by the


State Department to the Icelandic


government clearly foreshadows a


settlement of outstanding questions


between Iceland and the United


States. These questions center


around air rights and bases acquired


by the United States under the


mutual defense agreement con-
cluded between the two countries
on July 1, 1s41.


The vital role which Iceland could
play in safeguarding the northern
Sea-lanes between North America
and the British Isles was so obvious
that when Nazi Germany violated
the neutrality of Denmark in the
spring of 1910, British and Canadian
forces occupied Iceland, both to
forestall a possible German descent
upon the island and to make use of
its facilities for aircraft and naval
vessels. Iceland, though virtually
independent since 1918, still retained
link with Denmark through COM
mon allegiance to the Danish Royal
House.


This Anglo Canadian occupation
did not sit we'll with the Icelanders,
who proclaimed themselves an in
dependent republic in 1941. BY that
time, though still technically neu-
tral, we were obviously intent on
saving Britain from the Nazi men,
ace, especially the U-boat blockade.
All this led to the American-Ice-
landic defense agreement previously
referred to, under which our forces
took over and developed ample air
bases, notably the big Keflavik Air
port near Reykjavik, the Icelandic
capital and metropolis.


Obviously, American interests
would be best served by continual
ton of these air facilities, and our
State Department opened negotia-
tions to this effect at the close of
the late war. However, these nego-
tiations not only encountered Ice
landic national susceptibilities but
also evoked the opposition of Soviet
Russia, which intimated that, If the
United States acquired permanent
base rights in Iceland, it might
counter by pressing Norway for
similar rights in its dependencies,
Spitzbergen and Jan Mayen, the
latter an island not far from Iceland,
which would straddle the northern
sea-laneS.


The upshot Of all this is the
current American proposal to the
Icelandic government, which pre-
sumably will result in an agreement,
because it has already been ap-
proved by the Icelandic Executive
Branch and needs only ratification
by the Althing or Parliament, which
is reported favorably disposed. The
arrangement provides for the with
draWal of all American military and
naval personnel from Iceland within
one hundred and eighty days from
the ratification of the agreement
and the turning over of the air
fields constructed by us to the Ice
landic government, but with the
proviso that American civilian per-
sonnel be retained, that our civilian
aircraft enjoy their use along with
those of other nations, and that our
military and naval aircraft shall
enjoy similar facilities "in connec-
ton with the fulfillment of our
obligations for maintaining control
agencies in Germany"

LONDON, Aug. 24.-A British
government dominated by men who
have punched time clocks them
selves scanned the nations labor
relations picture today and found
it bright on the whole, with a few
/. dark patches.


While there were no major strikes
such as the United States expert
enced in the coal, steel, automotive,
electric and railroad industries
there were in the first six months
of this year 1,173 work stoppages,
costing 1,166, 900 man-days.


Reporting these figures, the Min
lister of Labor noted that the aver
age number of workers involved
was fewer than $50. Most OF the
strikes were wildcat" with union
leaders. often closely afnliated with
the Labor party, joining employers
IN trying to stop them.


London Goes without Milk.
A typical example was the strike
of plant workers that caused nearly
a million London suburbanites to
go without milk this week end. Ask
ing $24 for a 40-hour week, the men
stayed out despite union condemna-
ton of their stand as 'irrespon-
sible."


All told, 287 200 workers had been
on strike at one time or another
from January to June-fewer than
the number involved in the Ameri-
can soft-coal strike alone. OF them,
225,600 were In the key engineering,
iron and steel, coal mining and
shipbuilding industries.


Most of these disputes were set
tied quickly and caused no such
public inconvenience as did strikes
by dock workers, meat handlers,
Ulster bank workers and bread de-
liverymen, and London gas workers
who twice returned the capital to
wartime dimout conditions.
Despite the strikes, industrial pro-
duction scared and Britain's exports
for July reached the postwar record
figure Of 1857, soc, ,0O0-20 per cent
above the 1888 monthly average but
still SIS per cent short OF the Gov-
ernment's goal.


Many Refuse to Stay at Work.


Friends of the Labor government
saw in these figures an indication
that. the working man was respond
ing Fundamentally to pleas for
higher production, even though his
wages were not keeping pace with
the sky-high costs Of all but the
bare necessities.


But critics noted that large num-
bers Of workers were ignoring the
stay-at-work advice OF their union
leaders and asked what hold the
unions would have on their mem
bers when the major industries are
nationalized and millions work for
the government"


The chronically ailing coal mines,
soon to become the first nationalized
industry. seemed likely to provide
an answer. As many factories con-
verted from coal to Oil, the Fuel
Ministry predicted tight squeeze
this winter If no strikes occur
and God help u.s. said one official

Wonderful, Indeed, Is Progress
To the Editor Of The Star:


Laura K. Pollock planitively inquiries
In The Star about what has become of
the city's white wings"


Let her take heart Let her shout
with joy! Progress is here and we don't
need whitewings any more, with or
without creeping paralysis. The city
now sends large gray trucks through
the streets, instead. The trucks shoot
a strong blast of water directly at the
gutter. The force of the water lifts
trash from the days official trash COL
lection, etc, about 3 feet into the
air and with much splushing deposits
all this debris right smack on our
pavements.


Well, sir, we housewives, needing the
keep our streets clean" slogan, then
rush out with our respective brooms
and dustpans and, singing a roundelay,
gratefully sweep up all that Shiny,
smelly wet stuff the "sprinklers" slyly
left us. We empty the stuff in our trash
bins and, come the next trash collection
day, We find that the trash collectors
have left a goodly part of their take"
in the gutter, including part of the
muck We previously had removed from
the pavement.


Just after the trash collectors depart,
what do our listening ears hear but
the good old street sprinkler coming
down the street.


Hooray! They did it again!


Loan me your broom, Miz Jones,
please; mines worn clean down to a
stump"


Progress, it's wonderful

Of proposed treaties with former
enemy states in Europe.


French sources said sharply di-
vergent views were expressed this
afternoon at the deputies second
meeting of the day after all four
had agreed at morning session to
release for publication the agreed
portions of the Italian treaty before
the opening of the general peace
conference Monday.


Ultimate Result Not Clear.


Acting on this agreement concern
Ing the Italian pact, the British
Central Information Office dis
tributed the agreed sections for
publication at pm. eastern STAN
dard time) tomorrow in Washing
ton, London, Paris and Moscow.


just how the split among the
deputies which developed this after
noon would affect the ultimate de-
cision on publication of the italian
text was not clear tonight. In the
meantime, the American delegation
which has sought to release all sec
tions of all treaties was hampered
in communications with Washing
ton by sunspots which caused a
transatlantic radio jam. A courier
with the documents missed the
morning plane for the United
States.


Following their agreement on the
italian text, the deputies met again
to decide their policy on treaties
with Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria
and Finland. The Americans,
French sources said, pressed for re-
lease of all sections of all treaties to
both the press and official delega-
tions from the former enemy States.


Dispute on U. s. Reservation.


The British wanted only the
agreed portions given to the press
while both the agreed and unagreed
sections went to the delegations
The Russians, the French inform
ants said, were willing to publish
nearly all agreed and unagreed sec
tions. but demurred at publication
Of an American reservation on the
Hungarian treaty.


This reservation, 1t was reported,
applies to Article 21 which deals
with reparations. The Russians
wanted this article published with
out the reservation. thus giving the
impression the Americans had
agreed to it.


The Americans insisted on pub
fishing the reservation along with
the article. The French deputy for
eign minister tried to reconcile the
various viewpoints and, failing, the
deputies adjourned until tomorrow
without clear decision.

GUAM. Sunday, Sept. GA ty-
phoon that smashed the United
States Army's big air base here
and wrought havoc throughout the
fortified Marianas blew on north
westward today.


At least one Army man, who suf-
fered broken back, was injured
seriously. and 10 per cent of the
housing for Army dependents either
was destroyed or damaged. The
prodigious job of assessing the full
loss still lay ahead, however.


The Army's Harmon Field, hard
est hit of all the military installa-
tions, was so badly battered it was
ordered closed for 48 hours. Air
fields on the Northern end of Guam
nearest the typhoon center, also
were damaged extensively.


| Aircraft Service Unit IL reported
from the naval air base that 10 per
cent of its aircraft was damaged and
the control tower was demolished.


Full Accounting Waits.


Personnel was put on two meals
day. Power still was not restored
last night. Cloudbursts pouring
down on damaged and leaking quon-
set huts added to the discomfort.
Rear Admiral Charles A. Pownall,
commander of the Marianas, said
broken communications prevented
a full accounting, but no serious in
juries to naval, marine or civilian
personnel had yet been reported.


The 10O-mile wind subsidized BY
late yesterday, but 15-foot breakers
still lashed the shore.


Admiral Pownall said he had no
reports from Saipan, $50 miles north
Of Guam, but believed it had not
experienced as much damage as did
Guam.


The little island of Rota, so miles
north Of Guam. was in the direct
center of the storm, but Admiral
PoWnall said cave there was large
enough to shelter the entire popula-
ton of $50 persons plus the handful
Of military personnel stationed there.


The main weather station on
Guam was knocked out, virtually ali
communications lines were down
and the Navy radio station was
lnoperable for several hours.
Breakwater Punctured.


The naval hospital was among
buildings damaged Sheet iron
sheathing of many quonset huts
whirled through the air like leaves.
The newly completed multimil-
lion-dollar breakwater at Apra
Harbor was punctured in several
places, but the damage was re-
garded as relatively minor. ~


Although the typhoon was a
freak, which turned on the Mari
anas after having been plotted on
a course which would have missed
them, there was sufficient warning
for many precautions.


Wives and children of service
personnel were removed from quon-
sets to stouter buildings, most air.
craft were flown to Palau and ships
were ordered to put to sea.

CHANG CHUN, Manchuria
April 15.-A battle for Chang
chun was under way today be-
tween Chinese government and
Communist forces.


The Communists launched an at
tack yesterday two hours before the
final withdrawal of Soviet occupa-
ton forces from this Manchurian
capital.


The Communists already had
gained control of all three airflelds
in this vicinity and sifted into the
city from the suburbs.


Gunfire has been constant for the
last 10 hours.


The Communists were making de-
termined attacks from the north,
northwest and south. They began
shortly before Russian Maj. Gen.
Fedor Karlov left aboard his two
car, two locomotive special train for
Harbin.


Aerial Supplies Cut Off.


BY 10:30 o'clock last night the
Communists had captured the main
northwest airfleld, cutting off aerial
supplies for the small Chinese gov
ernment garrison.


The Government forces already
were short of ammunition.


In overrunning the airfeld, the
Communists captured an American
two-seater observer plane in which
Maj. Robert B. Rigg of Chicago ano
Sergt. Clay Pond of Portland, Greg.
had flown here Saturday.


Because Of broken communica
tions, the five American CORE
spondents here pooled their re-
ports to get this dispatch through
jointly.


The five are Tom Masterson OF
the Associated Press, George Wei
Ter of the Chicago Daily News
Henry R. Lieberman of the New
York Times, Reynolds Packard o1
the United Press and Charlotte
Ebener of the International News
Service.


Reserve Main Strength.


The Chinese government garri.
son, led by Maj. Gen. Chen Shin.
tsen, was reversing its main strength
for defense of the center of the
city, which is honeycombed with slit
trenches, barbed wire ENHANCEMENT
road blocks, and sandbagged ano
stone-heaped machine-gun emplace-
ments.


Sandbags were piled high in front
of a number of buildings, especial
ly the Central Bank Building, which
is being used as government military
headquarters.


The defending Peace Preservation
Corps, including green local re-
cruits built around a force of 1900
regulars, was flown in from Peiping
several months ago.

Mrs. Bayard Evans, who lives near

foot plunge into an abandoned well

friends in a woods near her home.


Less fortunate was her mount, q
12-year -old pony, who fell through
the rotting boards covering the well,
but was pulled to the surface appar-
emily uninjured, two hours later.


Mrs. Evans said she was riding
along a little-used trail when the
pony plunged through the boards.
Just as the animal fell, she said,
she was thrown clear.


A fire rescue squad nearby tried
in vain to extricate the pony. A
telephone company truck with
equipment to lift poles was more
successful, and after man had
been lowered into the well to fasten
ropes on the animals feet, 1t was
lifted to safety.


The pony, Mrs. Evans revealed,
belongs to her son Ralph, IL.

HAIFA, Palestine. Aug. 13.-
British troops fired Tommy guns
and rifles today into crowd
OF rioting Jews who were trying
to storm through tanks, trucks
and soldiers in protest against
the deportation to Cyprus of
1000 illegal Jewish immigrants.


A girl was killed. Several police
men and troops were injured by
stones, bottles and other missiles
which the Jews hurled soon after
the outlawed Hagana radio exhorted
them to storm the streets"


A moving tank injured one per-
son in dispensing a crowd gathered
in the Hadar Hacarmel quarter OF
this northern Palestinian port.


Two troopShips sailed with the
thousand illegal immigrants dur
ing the morning, but another ship
the sloop Fenice-bearing $50 Jewish
immigrants without landing GER
tifiicates arrived and was placed
under watch outside the harbor.


An unconfrmed report said yet
another illegal ship. the Venezia
which was spotted yesterday, had
arrived off Haifa with 900 more
illegal immigrants.


Violated Curfew.


The young Jews violated a cur
few TO demonstrate against the de-
oortations However the rioting
ahated and the curfew was lifted
this afternoon Police reported the
city was quiet at pm. as British
soldiers began Withdrawing.


The Hagana radio had called On
residents of Haifa to break the cur
few. which the British imposed
while the Jews were being loaded
for deportation.


Even the Arab quarters in Haifa
Joined in defiance of the curfew
The Arabs. however. caused little dis
turbance and ventured only outside
their own homes.


Several truckloads of youthful
men and women were taken to police
detention camps in Haifa for break
ii:g the curfew


AS noon approached police and
helmeted soldiers strung barbed-
wire barricades at virtually every
street intersection and appeared to
have restored a measure of order.


In other parts of Haifa feeling
was running high. but apparently
there was no concerted move to join
the rioters in the lower part of the
city.


1000 Confined in HarbOr.


The arrival of the additional i'm
migrants brought to more than
1000 the number of unscheduled
Jewish wanderers confined in the
Hsifa Harbor. even with the de-
portation of the 1000. Only 1900

British rules


The Fenice several weeks ago
brought another cargo of Jews from
La Spezia in Italy. The sloop had
been allowed to depart from Haifa
because its passengers received land
ing certificates and thus were not il
legal.


The Fenice apparently tried to
land its passengers on the beach but
was intercepted by police gunboat.
1t refused an order to heave to and
the gunboat fired across its bow. The
sloop was anchored outside the har-
Dor and its passengers, under the
new British policy, probably will be
deported.

hillside streets toward the docks
few minutes after the last refugees

The lst Infantry Division, called

Publication of the text of a state
ment by the Allied Commission for
Observing the Greek Elections gives
authoritative and unbiased informa-
ton regarding the character of those
elections. There can be no reason
able doubt as to the competence of
the commission for its task and the
validity of its conclusions. It should
be remembered that the commission
itself grew out of the Yalta Confer
ence whereat America, Britain and
Soviet Russia mutually agreed to
help liberated countries set up DEM
ocratic governments Furthermore,
this was followed by an agreement
between the Greek political parties
to seek such Allied help through
election observa ton, and the Greek
government subsequently requested
such aid from the Yalta signatories,
together with France. All accepted
save Soviet Russia, which declined to
participate and indicated it's dis
approval of Greek elections at this
time. The same attitude was taken
by the Greek Communist party,
which, together with some small
left-wing groups under its control
boycotted the elections and tried to
make others do the same.


Notwithstanding these handicaps,
the commission, composed of Ameri-
can, British and French observers
aggregating about 1900 and all care
fully selected for their jobs, reached
Greece some time before the elec-
tions, made prediction studies,
watched the actual polling, and con-
Quoted postelection hearings and
Investigations. They have now COM
pleted their report, which is signed

LONDON, June 8.-Ten million
Britons thronged London today to
celebrate the Allied victory in World
War II and all were determined to
make the most of this first formal
public rejoicing In Britain in nearly
10 years., 49,. %. %, ..


Among all the wartime Allies, only
three nations were not represented:
The Soviet Union, Yugoslavia and
Poland. These had notified the
British government earlier that they
would not send contingents. A
small group of Polish airmen who
had flown with the Raj appeared
with Britain's flyers, however.


Although the flags of those coun-
tries were not borne in the process
sion, they were fiowns conspicuously
from Poles along the mall and dis

Hours before dawn crowds jock

marchers and mechanical might led

notables.

mall along st. James Park, where

text:
Remembering Star Mary


To the Editor of The Star:


Recurrence Of Flag Day seems an
appropriate moment in which to con-
slider the saga of Star Mary, to pay .
tribute of respect to one of Washing
tons most colorful characters.


She was known by no other name
than Star Mary, mainly for the reason
that her only means of support came
from the sale of The Star on the streets.
She was Washington's first female
"newsboy"


Whence Mary came, and where and
when she vanished from the scene, no.
body seems to know. She never talked
about herself; never asked for sympathy
or charity. All she wanted was the
chance to make an honest living for
herself and the opportunity to follow .
parade whenever the occasion arose.


Among Star readers there must be
many whose memories reach back to
the Washington Of yesterday, when the
era OF street parades was in its heyday
and when no parade was considered
complete until Mary and her little
wagon of Stars closed in, waving her
little cotton flag, with the kindly cheers
OF the sidewalk spectators following her.


On Decoration Days indefatigable
Star Mary followed the procession to
Arlington, valiantly trundling her wagon
through the heat and dust, and she
a tn ba
Marine Band had played its last march
and taps" had echoed over the green
hills.


She was tiny, resolute figure who
contributed much to our best American
traditions of simple, down-to-earth pa
triotism.


What especial instinct of early train
ing first turned Mary to her own espe-
cial brand Of patriotism, nobody seemed
to know. There were few people who
shrugged their shoulders when she
passed, with the remark: ooh. that's
only old Star Mary. She's little crazy
over the flag, but perfectly harmless"


Maybe she was crazy, but so also then
were Betsy Ross and Molly Stark and
Barbara Freitchie and Clara Barton and
Mabel Boardman, for their lives and
achievements were cast from the same
pattern and nodded in the same form.


On Flag Day it seems fitting that the
old Washington Of yesterday should
pause to consider old Star Mary in her
black WOODEN shawl, the hag-wavingest,
most patriotic citizen Wsshinrton has
produced. LOUISE Z. SPERRY,
headline: Remembering Star Mary

beginning of tire rationing. But

United States cities. Now, the

In spirit of gratitude and

marked by a lack of riotous
revelry that had been expected
for the first peacetime New Year
eve in five years.


While most night clubs, hotels
and theaters did capacity business

away, and the celebrations gener-
ally were good-natured, rather than
boisterous.


It was the same on downtown
streets. Fair-sized crowds were out,
but for the most part they were
orderly and well behaved. Police
had little trouble in handling the
few boisterous celebrants.


Wars Toll Fresh in Minds.


The good-natured revelry seemed
to stem from feeling Of gratitude
that the war was over. Some point
ed out, too, that the conflicts toll
OF dead and manned was too fresh
in the public's mind for an unre-
strained celebration.


Convalescent Navy and Marine
Corps personnel welcomed the New
Year at party staged for them at
the Navy Medical Center, Bethesda,
Md, which was broadcast.


Watch night services were held
in many churches last night, and
today all Catholic and many Prot
estant churches were to hold spe-
cial services.


The general scene last night was
far different from VI night when
the celebration sometimes verged
on riotousness


One thing different from similar
celebrations during the war years
was the reduced number of service
men participating in the public fes-
tivity. However, there still was a
goodly number of soldiers. sailors,
Marines, WAVES and WACS in the
crowd.


Police said the celebration was
a bit more spirited than during the
war, but agreed that 1t fell far short
OF the New eYar eve sprees of the
good old" 1905. Six hundred
policemen were on duty between
midnight and / am.

police said Washington was "quieter

Grand Central Terminal was

1t was with some difficulty that

Pennsylvania Station.


The traffic snarl was occasioned

Word Received Late.

began.


Thomas J. Harkins, Eastern rep

would be at last eight hours-some
time after midnight-before normal
passenger service was restored.

difficulties for suburban residents

get home from Manhattan. Only
few of the trains which daily
carry millions into Westchester

postponed.

BOMBAY, Sept. 6.-The govern
ment announced tonight that for
the first time in the six days of
the city's bloody Hindu -Moslem
riots, violence showed a steady de-
cline all day. Nevertheless, IL per-
sons were killed and "A wounded
during the day.


Total casualties in nearly a week
of street battles stood tonight at
214 dead and 642 wounded.


Troops and armed police took up
positions to guard the mosques and
the routes leading to them and con-
tinued the anti-riot patrols which
they have carried on almost with
out rest since the Hindu-M -Moslem
fighting began. This was consid-
cred the critical day in the dis
turbances, one which might lead the
teeming city back to normal-or to
worse disorders.


Populace Less Jittery.


A group of correspondents who
toured the city during the morning
noted the populace seemed less jit-
terry than on previous days, but
stray stabbings continued through
the early hours, although some mills.
shops and factories reopened with
reduced stats.


The correspondents we're informed
of the heroism of one Hindu who
rescued two Moslem children from
hooligan mob. Other acts Of in
tercommunal assistance also were
reported.


I. I. Chundrigar. president of the
Bombay Provincial Moslem League,
issued statement advising Moslems
to "try to maintain peace and tram
quality but in case of attack to
keep themselves ready for self
defense"


Curfew Helps Restore Quiet.


The widely imposed curfew helped
quiet much Of the city during the
night, but stealthy stabs in the
back and knife slashings killed q
and wounded SO yesterday before
curfew, a government announce
ment said. Gunflre sounded several
times as police and troops battled
mobs attacking places of worship
in attempts to set them aflame.


At curfew time, exhausted police
vigorously drove everyone inside,
but the citys streets remained lit
tered with debris from looted shops
and foul stencil rose from long
uncollected refuse in the cutters.


During the night, any one who
had to be out walked carefully, and
only with trusted companions. They
avoided the doorways and alley en-
frances so often used by deadly
knife -wielders in their hit-and-run
attacks.

The House Civil Service Commit
tee today approved legislation which
would grant job promotions to new
Government employees who were
forced to decline appointments to
Federal jobs during the war be-

trict police and firemen.

ply to persons who passed civil serv-
ice examinations and were on the
eligible list waiting for jobs when
they entered the military service.


At present, these persons are en-
titled to get the job they competed
for, but they are denied any promo
tions they might have received had
they been In the Federal service
from the start.


Compare Other Promotions.

the advancements received by per-

since the time the veteran has been

tirement benefits to heads of execu-
tive departments and independent
agencies in the Government. At

cred by the Retirement Act. The
bill does not include cabinet officers.

annuity rights to Government en-
ployes with IS or more years Of
service who have been dismissed

Management won't be anxious to lose
their services. Experience has exploded
the old theory of male superiority in
every type of activity and demonstrated
that women are much better than men
at some things. They have smaller and
more dextrous hands, an advantage on
the average production line, and they
are less apt to be bored by monotonous
tasks. They have proved there is .
place for them in factories, even as
they proved that before in Offices and
stores. The fact seems to be that with
industry gradually settling back to a
peacetime normal, some women will
leave the factory for the home. but
great many others, both married and
single, will not. The war has set
pattern which will henceforth see more
women doing what, until Hitler's armies
marched into Poland, was traditionally
regarded as mans work.

TABRIZ, Iran, Dec. 13 (De-

Tabriz, impeding the entry of
government troops who reached
the borders of the Azerbaijan
provincial capital four hours ago.


Sacrifices of sheep and cattle were
offered by the roadside in the paths
of the slowly advancing army.


After a few days Of precarious
law and order, during which 10 per-
sons were reported killed amid in
discriminate shooting, the city be-
came quieter this afternoon with
the approach of government secur-
ity forces.


Resisting members Of the ousted
Democratic Party were driven from
their hiding places and, with hands
bound, were led off to jails.

Shops reopened during the day.
Young men, shouting and singing,
paraded through the city. waving
flags and displaying pictures of the
Shah.


Just one year after its formation,
the Azerbaijan provincial govern
ment. established under the Soviets
during their army's occupation sof
Northern Iran, had been overthrown.


DR.. Salamollan Javid, Governor
General of Azerbaijan, and Naji
Mira Shabastari, president Of the
provincial council, went to meet the
advancing government army.


A Soviet plane which had been at
Tabriz for week departed Thurs
day.


After the provincial government
and armed forces disintegrated, their
weapons fell into the hands of cit
izens. and firing started in the city
Wednesday night. For the next two
days rifle and machine-gun fire was
heard throughout the city almost
continually, especially around the
prisons and army barracks.

Thursday afternoon correspond
ents touring the streets were cheered

the army which left Mianeh Thurs

NUREMBERG, Oct. l2.-Col. Gen
Alfred Jodl, sentenced to die on the
gallows as war criminal next week,
bade his wife an impressive farewell
in his tiny cell today.


CAPT. Sam Binder of Woodbine,
Iowa, a security officer of the Palace
of Justice Jail, told reporters that
Adolf fditler's former chief of staff,
wearing the red-striped trousers and
dress coat Of a Prussian officer, was
calm and fearless during the hour
long visit.


Undoubtedly Frau Jodl told her
husband that his plea for clemency,
like all others from the IL doomed
NazisS had been denied by the Allied
Control Council in Berlin. Officials
here have been unable to tell the
prisoners so because they have not
been advised officially.


10 Convicted by Court.


Representatives of the council
were expected here from Berlin over
the week end to make arrangements
for the hangings, presumably set
for dawn Wednesday. The doomed
men were among 10 convicted by an
International Military Tribunal
which acquitted three others here
October 1.


Most of the condemned Nazis have
seen their wives for the last time.
Strain is showing on all of them
now. Their reactions are taking pc
culiar twists.


Rudolf Hess, Hitler's one-time
deputy, facing a life term, talks Of
organizing another Reich. He has
mentioned this several times to pris-
on doctors.


Hess complained to prison oficials
that he was getting "too much meat"
In his diet and would like to swap
some of it for prunes.


Capt. Binder said II assure you

planning that the Nazi prisoners get
one big meal daily at noon, coffee
and bread for breakfast and light
snack for supper.

Julius Streicher, Jew batter, asked
q psychologist to visit all the others
who must hang and tell him how
they were taking the approach of
death. Hans Frank, once governor
of Poland, greets his doctor daily
with: How are you feeling?"


wilhelm Frick, who was protector
of Bohemia and Moravia, has con-
cluded that "all is finished and there
isn't much use in waiting around. !"
Fritz Sauckel, former labor boss, has
cracked wide open and doesn't seem
to realize the trial is ended.


Field Marshal Wilhelm Keitel,
former Grief of the general stan,
sleeps well. Alfred Rosenberg, Nazi
philosopher, constantly PAGES his
cell.


The prison still houses Franz Won
Papen, acquitted German diplomat,
who can't seem to get an answer
from the British on his appeal to
enter their occupation zone.

Confirmation by our State De-
partment that the United States
and Britain have entered into for
NAL negotiations with Portugal for
continuous use of the air and naval
bases acquired on wartime leases is
important news from several as
poets.


The immense strategic value of
those bases was demonstrated dur
ing the war. Indeed, it was the OBJ
vious need for such Allied footholds
which prompted their acquire
ment. The Azores are not COM
pact archipelago. Instead, they are
a long string of islands with such
wide gaps between the several links
that the entire chain stretches al
most thousand miles, from point
not so very far from the Iberian
Peninsula of Europe to a point in
midAtlantic, virtually on the lati-
tude of New York They thus strad-
die the main sealane between our
east coast ports and the entrance
to the Mediterranean at Gibraltar,
and likewise flank the lanes from
South America to all points on
Europe's Atlantic coasts.


From the beginning of the late
war the German U-boat menace
grew in acuteness until it began to
decline with the perfecting of Al
lied joint naval and air patrols over
the Atlantic. However, their was one
gap in the netWork-the Azores. So,
in October, l943, the granting of
bases in the Azores by Portugal was
announced. This not only perfected
the antisubmarine Allied patrol but
also opened the way for that pre-
dominantly American invasion of
Europe which was then on the cards.


The agreement itself was nego-
tiated by the British government
under its more than 500-year treaty
relationship with Portugal, though
the United States shared in the
benefits. The present negotiations
for the perpetuation of the existing
base status, being conducted simul-
taneously by the United States and
Britain, indicate close and continu-
ing Anglo-American joint strategic
liaison over the entire North
Atlantic.


Indeed, this joint action regarding
the Azores is merely part of much
larger strategic liaison which covers
the entire Atlantic and Pacific
Oceans. We saw this only recently in

CHUNGKING, Mar. 23-Tht
Chinese government announced
today that Russia had promised
to withdraw all Red Army troops
from Manchuria by April 80. as
reports circulated that Chinese
Communists were maneuverine
to move in behind the Russians


Relief was expressed over the
Russian note, but the domestic
scene was darkened by growing evil
dence of nonco-operation between
the Communists and Generalissimo
Chang Kai-shek's Kuomintang.


Foreign Minister Wang shih-
chieh told the Peoples Political
Council that Russia had delivered
Friday the long-awaited reply to a
Chinese note asking when the Red
Army would carry out its agree
ment to quit Manchuria.


Promises Written Report.


Wang, pressed for details, prom
tsed to furnish written report of
negotiations over Manchuria, a SUBJ
'ject concerning which the govern
ment has been highly secretive.


Government sources said it was
unlikely that the Soviet troop with
drawal would apply to Dairen or
Port Arthur, where Russian rights
have been established by treaty.
Both are heavily garrisoned by Rus
slams.


The Central News Agency said
5000 Chinese Communists had fl
tered into the Northern Manchurian
city of Harbin. The World Daily
News charged that Communist
troops were massing in neighboring
Jehol province.


Other Chinese dispatches report
ed a column of government troops
was marching on Communicated
SSepingkai, railway city 100 miles
north of Mukden.


Chungking Sources Pessimistic.


These accounts said all Chinese
government-appointed officials for
Heilungkiang, northern province
whera the Communists have been
reported setting up an independent
regime, would leave Changchun,
Manchuria's capital, for Peiping be-
cause they were unable to assume
their duties.


Foreign diplomatic sources in
Chungking took an extremely pes
simistic view of the internal situa-
tion. They said Gen. George C.
Marshsll's personal influence was
the dominating factor in forcing
the Communists and the Kuomin-
tang to sign the recent unification
agreement and without him on the
scene> "the situation is rapidly get
ting out of hand"


Foreign observers asserted that
both the Communist and Kuomin-
tang factions were taking advantage
of the special American envoy's alb
sence in Washington.

The United Public Workers of
America (CIO) today claimed its
membership has jumped by $4,000
persons since its initial convention
last April, making it 1.-The largest
public service union in the country"


The union said its membership
now numbered 100000 persons in
good standing" compared to the
$4,000 total when the United Fed
eral Workers of America merged
with the State, County and Munich
pal Workers of America at the At
lantic City convention.


The figures occasioned consider
able surprise since the new union
has been sharply attacked in Con-
gress and other high places ae a
left-wing organization as a result
OF its pro-Soviet foreign policy reso-
luton and thescontroversy over it's
strike policy. Some observers felt
the no-strike rider adopted by Con-
gress would frighten some members
away from the organization even
though the union at the last minute
revised its strike policy to meet the
terms of the amendment.


Some Losses Here.


Donald Murray. legislative officer
OF the union, said there had been
some losses in membership in some
agencies here, but that gains in
other bureaus had Offset these losses.
He said it was in cities outside
Washington that the union made
Its real membership gains.


Seventeen new Federal locals have
been formed throughout the United
States, Mr.. Murray said. However,
about two-thirds of the $4,000 gain
In membership resulted from the
signing Of employees in municipalities
and State governments, it was said.
The largest single gain in men,
bership was in Detroit where the
union won a special bargaining
election from several other unions
involving 1000 employees of the citys
| department of public works.


| Most of the new Federal workers
signed up are employees of the Vet
Grams Administration, National
Housing Agency, the Office of Price
Administration and various Naval
Air Stations, 1t was said.


Drops in Two Departments.
The membership dropped some
what IN the Agriculture and Treas
ury Departments here. Probable
reason for the drop in the Agricul-
ture Departments membership was
the fact that the first no-strike rider
was attached to its appropriations
bill. 1t wasn't until last week that
the union clarified it's no-strike
policy, and undoubtedly some of its
members at Agriculture dropped out
for fear they would lose their Jobs.
The rider. which has been tackled on
all agency appropriation bills, bars
employment Of any persons belong
ing to union which asserts the
right to strike against the Govern
ment.


The unions Executive Board met
last week and mapped plans ito
double" the membership during the
next two years. Mr.. Murray said he
hoped the goal could be met, adding
that "our membership gains since
April should encourage us in our
drive, since the $4,000 new members
were added without the benefit Of a
concerted membership drive or the
efficient organiZational setup that
we achieved at last weeks meeting"

MELBOUR RNE, Dec. 28.-The
windup of the Davis Cup challenge
round, postponed by heavy rains
until Monday, was saved from being
pure anti-climax today by the de.
cision of Australia's John Brom.
wich to return to play.


Bromwich Withdrew yesterday
after he and Adrian Quist sur
rendered to the United States the
trophy Australia as held since 1886
in losing the decisive doubles match
to the American team of Jack Kra-
mer and Ted Schroeder.


Schroeder had started the rout
the previous day by trimming Brom-
wich at singles and Kramer followed
through with a three-set victory
over Dinny Pals.


The remaining two singles
matches, which will have no bearing
on the final outcome, were scheduled
for today, but the Kooyong Courts
were drenched after an all-night
rain, and a heavy downpour as
play was about to start forced the
postponement.

playing Captains Walter Pate
of the American team and Gerald

eyed. 4-month-old baby girl taken
with its carriage from outside a
near North Side department store
while her mother shopped yesterday

eral miles away in a nursery at
Union Station.

child apparently had been placed in
a bed in the railroad stations
nursery while an attendants back
was turned, several hours after the
baby was reported missing. The
carriage also was found in the depot,

as Miss Evelyn Pleshko, Is, the
mother of the baby, reported to
police the child and carriage were
gone when she emerged from a half
hours visit at Milwaukee avenue
store.

first said her name was Mrs. EVELYN
Lieberman and that she had a
husband living in Detroit, but later
said these statements were not true,


The police investigation of the
incident will continue. Capt. Enright
said.

WASHINGTON, Pa, Feb. 23-A
woman was killed and A other per-
sons injured, five of them seriously,
in a boiler explosion which rocked
the First Christian Church during
q Washington's birthday father
and-son banquet last night.


There was no fire and, after the
first shock, the group of some 200
persons who were uninjured left the
church dining room in an orderly
manner.


Washington Hospital, where the
injured were treated, identified the
dead woman as Mrs. Martha Knes-
trick Mollenauer, 81, church organ
ist. The explosion occurred as she
walked past the boiler room door.
She was struck by pieces of the
boiler and died about two hours
later.


The interior of the church was
wrecked. The partition between the
boiler and dining rooms was fat
tened and part of the dining room
ceiling fell.

Bog mice prefer the open bogf


to be found mostly in woodland


clearings They live in runways


close to the surface, or they establish
residence in dense patches of grass


Their nurseries are unusually under


fallen log.


Usually these small creatures keep


well out of sight, scurrying from


one place to security to another


Lumbermen have seen large num-


bers Of them dart from their retreats


when q tree has fallen. Their pas
sage ways are long and many.
These mice are slightly over S


inches in length and are clothed
in bright chestnut fur suit with
many black hairs. The sides are
buff color, underneath white. The


tail is longer than that of . meadow
mouse.


In summer they gather seeds and
vegetables to see them through the
lean days. Their bins are located
in underground galleries. A long


hard winter may force them to
slaughter their weaker breathern.
During the winter when the bog
freezes over, the upper runways are
deserted for other places promising
warmth and shelter.


Young red-backed mice do not
have the bright red tints of their
parents. Some are clad in gray
birthday suits. They acquire the
more colorful costume later, al
though some stick to a gray suit
from birth to death.


Owls and hawks are adrent hunt
ers over the bogs for these swift
footed neighbors. The mice are very
prolific, but their enemies keep them
in check


A cousin often mistaken for this
bog traveller Is the one choosing the
very cold, damp sphagnum Of
southern New Jersey. He lives well
down in the moss sharing his large
runwaysl with the lemming and
meadow mouse as well as the tiny
shrews.

Carl Snyder, 76, nationally-known
author, economist, editor and Stats
tician, died here yesterday after a
long illness.


Born in Cedar Falls, Iowa, April
%, 1869, Mr.. Snyder entered news
paper work, becoming an editor at
Council Bluffs. Iowa, and later ar
editorial writer for the Washington
Post


He was educated at Iowa State
University, and early showed par
tiality for economic and statistical
problems which formed the chief
part of his life's work Among his
many books were New Conceptions
in Science" published about 1904
"The New World Machine" "Ameri-
can Railways as Investments, "
Business Cycles and Business
Measurements" and Capitalism and
the Creator"


Mr.. Snyder was former president
OF the American Statistical Associa-
ton and fellow of the American
Association for the Advancement of
Science and the American Academy
Of Arts and Letters.


He came here for his health about
three years ago and had lived in
semiretirement.

the Associated Press reported today.

told them she came from Washing
ton, but refused to give a street
address.


According to police, Mrs. Sabato
and man entered a midtown ap-
parel shop last night and held up
the woman manager, escaping with
SIS and handbag after throwing
pepper in the managers eyes.


Mrs. Sabato was arrested in the
lobby of a nearby hotel shortly after

found.

had not heard from their daughter
since she left their home at 3S13
Fortieth place, Colmar Manor. Mrs.
Findley said she and her husband
have not yet been notified by New
York authorities concerning Mrs.
Sabato's arrest.


Mrs. Sabato's aunt, Mrs. Louise
Houser, 423 Fourth street NV, said
her niece brought her three-year-
old son, George, to her last Novem-
Der and asked her to care for the
child while she went to work at the

When the first quarter of the year
has been checked off and times
wheel rolls into the fourth month,
the countryman knows that new
season has come to the land. Gone
is the March wind with her flip
pancies and teasing, her sudden
moods of i'll temper, her beWilder-
ingly benign interludes of sunny
disposition. April is the time when
spring work on the farm starts in
earnest.


On upland fields and slopes where
light soil dries out quickly the farmer
starts his spring plowing. 1t is work,
but task that many men enjoy.
There is something almost mystic
and ritualistic as the coldly moist
brown slices of sod curl away from
the glistening plowshare. The even
burrows make familiar pattern on
the earth as the steady plodding
team pulls the pillow back and forth
across the field. Reins hang loosely
from the farmers neck, he rarely
has to speak to the patient strong
horses. In good plowing it is easy
to guide the ploW, and at burrows
end the experienced horses take a
wide circling turn so that their
master does not have to haul the
plow around.


1t is season of promise. Through
the ages when spring has come
men have gone forth to prepare the
soil for seed, confident that in good
time the sun, warmth and moisture
would bring the harvest on which
mans food depends. There is
swelling chorus in the countryside.
Bluebirds carol their sweet senti-
mental arias, robins sing their
cheerful optimistic roundelays The
smaller brooks tumble down hillsides
and make music as they hurry along,
the creeks and meadow brooks
chuckle as their high waters push
along toward rivers and lakes. Buds
have broken their winter-t tight
stitching. Each day the sun circles
higher toward the pole of the hori-
IONS. The fourth month says winter
Is done and new season Is at hand.

NEW YORK, April 6.-Trainer
Tom Smith today held a favorable
legal decision in his long fight to
regain license to condition horses.


The appellate division of the
State Supreme Court yesterday
granted the veteran horseman a
stay of the Jockey Clubs order bar
ring him from all race tracks until
next November in connection with
the stimulation of the horse Mag
nific Duel at Jamaica last November.


The court denied Smiths appeal
for motion to direct the Jockey
Club to grant him 1916 license but
left the way open for him to apply
for a license from the Jockey Club.


Smith also had asked for an order
staying the suspension of his 1945
license but the court ruled this was
purely academic as the 1945 permit
expired last Sunday.


Smith, former trainer for the
highly successful Maine Chance
Farm, had his license revoked and
was suspended for one year when the
Jockey Club charged Magnif1c Duel
was sprayed with the drug ephre-
drine before winning race. Smith
based his appeal on the fact that a
groom in his employ administered
the stimulant without his knowledge.
Under racing rules, however. a
trainer is responsible at all times
for the horses in his charge.


The appellate court, in granting
Smith permission to re-enter race
tracks, ordered him to prepare for
a hearing of his appeal, from his
suspension on April %.

The thrush family contains birds
which know how to sing sweetly
There are hundreds of kinds of
thrushes.


Some say that hermit thrushes"
have the sweetest songs in the entire
family. These birds are called her
mlts because they like to spend their
time in the woods, away from people.


One bird expert speaks of the
hermit thrush as ''an unseen musi-
clan" and adds that it gives forth
sweet, silvery. bell-hke notes"
which are soft, low and tinkling at
the beginning, and rise higher and
higher"


Another fine singer is the wood
thrush This bird is, less timid than
the hermit thrush, and shows less
fear of being near people.


Wood thrusheS fly north with the
spring weather. They make their
nests in States, as well as in parts
OF Canada. Often they raise their
young in Northern Ontario. In the
United States they are found from
New England TO Minnesota, and
southward to Texas. Now and then
they make their homes west of the
Mississippi.


Less gifted as singers are the
mlssel thrushes of Great Britain and
the mainland of Europe. Missel
thrushes receive their name because
Of their fondness for the berries of
mistletoe plants.


Missel thrushes are small, but
sturdy fighters They show great
bravery when they defend their
nests and their young.
Magpies sometimes attack the
nests of missel thrushes. When this
happens, the parent birds come out
to night. Time and again they have
been known to drive away an attack
| ing magpie.

The eggs of the piping plover can
be found in the sandy beaches of
Southern Saskatchewan. Southern
Ontario, Magdalen Islands and from
Nova Scotia south to Central Ne
braska, Northwestern Indiana. Lake
Erie, New Jersey and Virginia.


This bird is rightly called the
beach, sand and clam plover. The
eggs, generally four in number, are
laid in fairly deep, Well-rounded
depression in clean sand. They are
not only found on the seacoast but
on sandy or pebbly shores of the
larger inland lakes. The eggs are
distinct from those of related spe-
cieS, being very finely freckled with
sepia, with a creamy white ground
color.


Piping plovers are 7 inches In
length and almost invisible unless
they pipe or move They have a
white forehead. a black band on
their crown from eye to eye and
their lores, chin, throat and sides of
head are pure white. Upper parts
are very pale ashy-brown. There
are black streaks, white spaces and
markings blended to make the bird
lnconSpicuous to all enemies. But
once you know this clam hunter.
you actually can spot him without
much trouble.


upon your approach all you see
is streak of something white pass
ing you and you hear the plaintive
piping call, as the bird goes swiftly
ahead.


At first the babies resemble small
punches of cotton batting blowing
over the hot sand Then you see
they are propelled by slender legs.


The food of the tiny plovers is the
minute marine life cast up by the
waves. Protection by law has been
flnally given these beautiful little
beach babies. Some of them become
quite tame with children who have
been with them as they grew up.
Even the parents in some locations
will stand quite close when other
clam hunters are present and accept
with alacrity those tossed to them
as neighborly Offering.

Though these are days to try mans
soul and peace may seem distant goal,
don't face each coming hour with dread
or let the blood rush to your head.
Don't long for castles fair in Spain,
just find a peaceful country lane and,
one by one, your worries drown while
roaming woodland paths adown.


Anemones nod tiny heads whene'er
you near their messy beds. Passing bees
hum, "Ah there, honey!" WELCOMED"
squeaks fleeting bunny. Birds in every
roadside tree chirp their greetings
neighborly and, as you reach the river
bend, the ripples murmur, "Howdy,
friend"


Those atom bombs may fall anon
and blow us all to Erehwon, but for the
nonce just feast your eye on yonder
lovely butterfly! RAY H. EVERETT.

public.

of the present Highway Bridge.

The Commissioners planned to
discuss the community-sponsored
project to convert E. v. Brown
School into a combined library
branch and recreation center at
their board meeting today.


Commissioner John Russell Young
said the project-aired at hearing
yesterday-would be reviewed at the
board meeting in preparation for
final decision from the District
Building.


Prompt Action Promised.


Assurance that the Commissioners
would act promptly on the proposal
came from Commissioner Guy Ma
son, who emphasized there would
be mo delaying tactics"


There's a new philosophy and
new policy to be determined here"
Commissioner Mason said.


Engineer Commissioner Gordon
R. Young said yesterdays hearing
was zone of the best presentations
I've ever seen"


The other Commissioners agreed
the arguments marshalled by Chevy
Chase residents and library and rec
reation officials were well organ
ized," and Commissioner John Rus
sell Young said the witnesses
brought out just what We wanted
to hear"


80 Witnesses Appear.


The Commissioners devoted more
than two and half hours to hear
ing proponents of the library-recre-
alton center plan. More than 80
witnesses appeared, either present.
ing detailed arguments and esti-
mated costs and savings or offering
brief Endorsements from the groups
they represented.


The city heads were obviously i'm
pressed by the size Of the delegation,
which included education, recrea-
ton and library officials; religious
leaders Of Chevy Chase, Boy and
Girl Scouts, parents, American Le-
gion representatives, merchants,
and students in the
Chevy Chase schools.

STERLING, Mass, April g.
Five children, left in care of a
young neighbor, perished early
today when fire swept their two
story frame dwelling.


They were identified by their
parents, Mr.. and Mrs. Francis
Woodring, as Winifred. 10: Patricia
and Priscilla, 8, twins: Francis
Michael, 6, and Carol Ann, S.


Four of the bodies were recov-
cred shortly after the blaze was
extinguished, but they were charred
beyond recognition. The fifth was
found several hours later.


A l5-year-old girl, Nancy Cut
Ter, who State police said was mind
ing the children while their parents
attended a basket ball game in
nearby Worcester, suffered burns on
the arms and hands.


State police quoted her as saying
the fatal fire broke out after she
had extinguished a slight blaze
earlier in the evening in the upper
floor where the children were
quartered.


After she doused the first blaze
with water, state police said she went
downstairs and fell asleep until she
was awakened by smoke, She re-
ported that flames and dense smoke
drove her back as she attempted to
ascend stairs to reach the young
sters.


She said she called the local tele-
phone operator before being driven
out by the blaze. When firemen
reached the scene the structure was
engulfed in flames.


The parents returned home shortly

Employees of the Army Finance

when it appeared that the time they
took to vote in the District plebis-

annual leave.


What made them especially angry
was the fact that their colleagues
from Maryland and Virginia are
being given the usual two hours off
to vote without time deduction.


When The Star called to check
this report, Army officials said the
order had been modified on receipt
of new War Department order and
that the employees would get an hour
off to vote without its being sub
tracted from their leave The en-
ployes will be permitted to end their
day at pm. instead of the usual
5 o'clock quitting time.


Army officials said the Maryland
and Virginia employees were given
the two-hour period because they
have longer way to travel" from
the Office to their voting places.

representatives and magnates next
Monday in New York.

has been elected to represent the
National League players on the
new Executive Council that replaced
the old Advisory Council, said there
were few differences of opinion on
the reforms.


A 5000 minimum wage, $25 per
week during spring training, elimi-
nation Of the To-day release clause
and pension and security fund are
the major points of the platform.

SANTIAGO, Feb. 4.-Activities in

today, three hours after the dead
line of scheduled general strike.


Socialist Labor leaders withdrew
their support Saturday, splitting the
once -united Labor Front Com
munist leaders insisted that the
strike 60 on as scheduled.

Confederation of Labor, urged work.
ers to remain on the job and to
"avoid provocation which might lead
to bloodshed."


The present labor crisis was
brought about by the action OF the
government last month in dissolving
the nitrate unions. A meeting pro-
testing the dissolution, held here
last Monday, resulted in the deaths
of six labor confederation members

day, contains six new members-four
Socialists and two former members
of the Radical party. Three mill
tary leaders, whose presence in the
old cabinet was protested by labor
groups, were retained in the new
cabinet along with one member of
the Popular Front and two ministers
without party afdliation.

er crossed the Greek frontier be-
fore withdrawing under fire.

Albanian border guards opened fire
on Greek guards on September 8.
On September 9, the Albanian con-
tingent took positions opposite the
Greek border guards and opened
fire with automatic weapons from
four different points"


Later" the report continued.
"the Albanian contingent entered
Greek territory to depth of 40
meters (about As yards but with
drew when fired at.


Before opening fire, the Alba
mans, using loud speakers, uttered
insults against Greece and fired
smoke missiles which burst near our
guards. Albanian losses are un-
known. One of our men was slightly
injured"


Specific Location Withheld.


The announcement did not state
specifically where on the Greek
Albanian border the attack occurred.


The Ministry also said a band of
900 Greek Communists today at
tackled a mountain village near Ka-
terini, south of Salonika, in the
Mount Olympus region. The Min
istry Of Public Order, however, said
it had no report of such an action.


Reinforcements were dispatched
from the three garrison towns of
Elasson, Larrissa and Tyrnavo and
the attack finally was repulsed, the
Press Ministry said.


New violence. including the Slay-

wounding of another, plagued
Athens today as military courts
sentenced two persons to death
under the drastic emergency powers
invoked by the government in its
attempt to quell alleged Leftist-
inspired disorders.


British military authorities said
bandits, dressed in uniform of the
Greek gendarmerie, ambushed five
British soldiers in a truck, killing
one and wounding another with
Bren and machine-gun fire.


Ty, Cot~ II 4

for throwing grenade into a pri-
vate dwelling and the other for
possession of explosives. A railway
bridge near Karditza in that area
was blown up yesterday and traf-

Leftist Editor Sentenced.

tor and four assistants of the Leftist
newspaper Laiki Foni to Jail for pub

establishment of the courts. The
editor was given a five-year term

year terms. The newspaper was
suspended for year.

ing in connection with the Staying

reference to the investigations.

TOKYO, Feb. 23.-The empress
of Japan walked among her nations S
sick and poor yesterday. She saw
unhappy, miserable people.


Saisekai Hospital and clinic for
the destitute evidently had been
prepared for Empress Magako's
visit. But no amount of work could
conceal dirty walls, gloomy corri-
doris, tattered linoleum. No amount
OF preparation could hide the mis-
cry of patients lying on unkempt
straw mattresses covered with
lumpy bedclothes in rooms where
radiators stood unused and cold.


The empress departure from the
moated palace to give personal SOL
ace to the victims of Japan's years
OF war followed by two days EN-
peror Hirohito's unprecedented two
day tour Of the bomb -f1attened To-
kyo area.


Rode From Palace.


She rode directly from the palace
to the hospital in a black Mercedes
Benz limousine, marked with the
imperial golden crysanthemum. She
wore a blue dress with a touch of
white at the throat, a black coat
with fur collar, black oxfords,
and black gloves. Her hair was
coiftured. American style, softly
waved and held in place by bobby
pins and black hairnet.


The royal party included Prince
Takamatsu, second eldest brother
of Hirohito..


Sympathetically, the Empress asked
about hospital conditions-how the
patients were treated, how they were
responding to treatment, if the
babies she saw were getting proper
feeding.


Supt. Takeo Koyama told her there
was not enough milk or medicines
and that patients responded slowly
to treatment because of improper
diet.


Talks With Nurses.


The Empress talked with nurses
whose hands were blue with cold,
with patients respectful but reluct-
ant to withdraw from bedclothing
cocoons from which they derived
scant warmth.


She watched the examination of
an elderly woman twitching with
cold and witnessed the bandaging
Of the arm of 13-year- -old boy.


A mother herself, the Empress
clucked at the infant in an iron
crib, smiled at small boy whose
right ear was bandaged.


Concluding the hospital tour, she
went to the roof. For blocks in
everysdlrection there were evidences
of destruction.


Overhead American airplanes
droned slowly.


Below in the rubble, Japanese
erected metal shacks and small
wooden frame buildings con-
quered. people attempting to renew
their slives.

AKRON, Ohio.-The rubber companies
are experimenting on the auto tire of
the future, casing that is hoped to run
100000 miles, or nearly the life of the car.


All these tire studies are secrets, and
are strictly laboratory experiments. How
ever, some have gone long way toward
the astonishing goal. BY all indications
this tire of the future will use both
synthetic and natural rubber.


The principles to make improved tires
are known throughout the rubber in
dustry.


The ideal tire would have almost no
weight, but very great elasticity. The
rubber laboratories never expect truly
weightless tire with perfect stretch, but
they have many plans for approximating
this dream.


Tires could be made stronger by
adding to their bulk and weight. But
the added bulk builds up extra heat
that would separate the plies and burn
out some of the other qualities.


One OF the great prewar advances in
the life of tires came when manufac-
turers went to thinner carcasses and
lower air pressures. That was an ex-
ample OF using less weight and more
elasticity IN certain parts Of tire.
