BALTIMORE, Mar. l2.-The Uni
versity of Maryland and Johns Hop
kins University medical and dental
schools shifting back to peace
time basis = will have fiye-month
vacations this year, but men SUBJ
ject to the draft are excepted from
the long holiday.


Abandoning their telescoped
three-year war schedules for the
normal four-year programs, the
universities will end an academic
year this month and start new
terms in September.


Selective Service regulations re-
quire that men who seek defer
ments, to continue their studies,
must be in school for nine months
Of the calendar year and take q
maximum of three months vaca-
ton. Special courses will be pro-
vided for these draftable men until
June.


Option Given Students.


University officials said that STU
dents not subject to the draft
either could enroll in special courses
or take q five-month vacation.


The gap in medical and dental
studies was caused by termination
of the Army specialized training pro-
gram this month, the officials
explained.


Maryland dental students ended
their course last Saturday, and
medical students enrolled by the
Army are scheduled to complete
their terms on March a.


Special Elective Courses.


At Hopkins, the medical school
year and the ASTP program will
end on March 10, and special elec-
tive courses will begin Immediately,
DR.. Alan Chesney, medical school
dean, said.


Members of freshman medical
and dental school classes will not be
affected by the long-vacation plan.
They began their present academic
year in September and will not end
it until June.


Selective service officials said the
new regulations did not require
draft-subject men to study under
accelerated courses, but they do de-
mand nine months of study a year.

The Governments reduction-in-
force program has revived a long
standing argument-whether an
employe with an agency 10 years
should be dismissed while the man
at the next desk who has been with
the same agency only a short time
but has longer Government service
is retained.


Both the War and the Navy De-
partments, with big staff cuts under
way, conceded today that some old
employees are being fired while COM
paratlvely recent employees hold
their jobs.


Regulation Cited.


Neither agency could estimate
how widespread this practice was,
but both pointed to the civil service
regulations providing that retention
IN a job was based on length of
service in the Government rather
than in an agency.


Employees who have been with an
agency for 10 years and now are be-
ing let out complain bitterly that
other employees, who transferred
from another agency during the war
and are being retained could 90
back to their old Government Jobs.


While this is possible. the Civil
Service Commission points out that
these new former jobs may no long
er exist. Some veterans already
have found that Government Jobs
they held before the war have been
abolished. Jobs have been changed
and whole sections wiped out, the
Civil Service Commission said. As
a result, their wartime jobs NAV
be the only one these employees
have.


A Navy Department personnel Of
f1cial pointed out that the old en-
ployes giving way to newer en-
ployes with longer Government sery-
ice were not the only old employees
hit by the reduction in force.


Different Levels.


This official said some engineers
who had been with the Navy 20
years were being fired while clerks
who had been with the Navy cnIy
few weeks were retained. This
comes about because they are on
different competitive levels. The en-
glneers who worked their way I'D
to high ratings over a period of
years simply are not in competition
with those on lower levels. If the
Navy needs fewer engineers. some
OF the old employees have to 60, the
Navy official said.


Under civil service regulations, re-
tention credits are computed by al
lowing one point for each full year
of Government service. In addi-
ton, five points are given for an
excellent" efficiency rating, but 10
points are awarded for any other
efficiency rating. These regulations
give less weight to efficiency ratings
and greater weight to length of
service-regardless of whether the
employe sat at the same desk for
10 years or served in two different
agencies.

day that "a few persons" have been
arrested in connection with the re-
moval of Benito Mussolini's body
from Milan potter's field.


Romita refused to identify the

want to interfere" with the inves-
tigation.


In Milan, Police Chief Umberto
Ferrante said two night watchmen
at the cemetery had been arrested,
but there was no indication whether
they were among the persons to
whom Romita referred. Ferrante
added that the investigation had
extended into the provinces far out
side Milan. Numerous gravediggers
have been questioned because the
exhumation was done with profess
sional skill, he said.


Romita denied reports that Musso-
lini's body had been given a secret
new burial at the former dictator S
birthplace at Predappio and as
serted there were no new clues to its
whereabouts.


In Rome, Italian police posted a
continual guard around the Palazzo
Venezia to thwart possible attempts
to slip the body into the Duce's for
mer headquarters.


Both Allied and italian vehicles
on the Rome-Milan highway were
carefully checked by police.


Rome newspapers meanwhile ques-
toned Romita's assertion yesterday
that "one man alone" knew the To-
cation of the unmarked grave from
which Mussolini's body was removed
Monday night. The papers asserted
that watchmen had unhesitatingly
pointed out the location to visitors
in the cemetery.

The Chapman Subcommittee

to the House Interstate and For

bill to construct twin four-lane
bridges across the Potomac River
to replace the Highway Bridge.


Meeting in closed session, the Ave
man group terminated more than
18 months of controversy over the
bridges.


Indications were the full commit
tee and the House would back the
committees stand, especially since
President Truman has said that he
favors the twin bridges rather than
a single bridge of six lanes.


S2,OO0,000 Available.


The bridge controversy, which
brought numerous clashes among
high Government officials, has gone
on since January 3, 1945. A 81, 900 900
initial appropriation made for this
year has remained unspent as the
District government and Public
Roads Administration and Fine Arts
Commission argued the matter out
with the National Park Service and
the National Capital Park and Plan
ming Commission. Civic and pro-
fessional groups Joined the dispute
from time to time.


Thousands of words of conflicting
testimony had been heard by the
subcommittee before it made its
decision today, with both sides ar
riving at different answers from vir-
tually the same set of traffic sta
tisticS.


Recognized Bottleneck.


The President entered the con-
troversy several months ago by GO
ing on tour of the bridge site. He
became the first President to ascend
to the top of the Washington Mon-
ument, going there to get birds
eye view of the congested river
crossing. The committee has made
two tours, one up the Monument.


All parties have agreed all along
on one thing-that the Highway
Bridge is one of the worst traffic
bottlenecks in the Washington ares.
Almost daily for the last few years
traffic has piled up when cars have
stopped for motor or tire trouble ;,
have run out of gas or have become
involved in collisions.


The bridges proposed in the bill
would cost $1,000 1000. The south
bound span would be built approx
imately at the site of the present
bridge and the northbound span
about 600 yards downstream, toward
the Railroad Bridge.

When spring comes, there are
many outdoor spots to revisit and
new ones to explore. But, there
is ever that fear about meeting
snakes. Let's settle that question
about water snakes.


In North America there are 10
species and several varieties. Eight
OF them occur east of the Mis-
sissippi River. These serpents are
common in the United States, Eu-
rope and Asia. They are recog-
nized by their stout bodies and
coarse scales.


Because they frequent the bor-
ders OF streams, lakes, rivers, ponds
and swampy places, they have been
correctly named water snakes. But,
they have been wrongly called


moccaslns." The true moccasins
belong in a very different group
and are deadly poisonous.


The banded water snakes habits
are similar to those of the tribe.
When disturbed they always take
to the water, even when stone piles
and underground are closer.


When cornered they assume a
pugnacious attitude, bite viciously
and poison the air with a fearful
odor. Their teeth can make slight
wounds, but these snakes have no
venom. Although these reptiles
rarely stroll from water, they are
perfectly contented without it in
captivity, so long as they have
enough to quench their thirst.


The banded water snake has a
stout body slightly over 3 feet long.
1t is dull in appearance due to the
coarse scales. The bands are not
distinctly outlined. On the sides
there are blotches of bright red
or yeIlowish- brown. Extending
across the back are narrow yellow
lsh bands. The abdomen has a
yellow cast and there are numerous
bright red blotches mingled with
spots of gray or black.


The mother may give birth to so
young at one time. She deserts
them Immediately. The youngsters
shed their birthday clothes shortly
after. Until they gain confidence.
they hide under chips and fiat
stones. Soon they may be seen
with their elders resting on the
branches of low trees and shrubs
overhanging the water At the
slightest annoyance, they drop be-
low and hide until their scare"
is over.

leaders back to-work orders.

to pay salaries for the strike period

return soon after the postal workers

end quickly thereafter.

unless their pay and working hours
are adjusted.

PEIPING, Oct. 5.-Generalissimo
Chang Kai-shek's chief Of stan,
Gen. Chen Cheng, flew to Peiping
to-day as Communist forces closed
In on Paoting, capital Of Hopeh
Province, and pushed government
troops from the outer defenses Of
that walled city.


Gen. Chen, accompanied by .
large staff, rushed here on Gen.
Chiang's orders to direct the Paoting
battle.


He called two extraordinary con-
ferences here of Gen. Chiang's top
military leaders In North China and
Manchuria, presumably to chart the
governments offensives against
Kalgan, Communist military base In
Chahar Province.


Thirteen thousand Red troops
were thrown In q tight circle around
Paoting, said the Catholic news
paper Social Welfare. As Commu-
nists penetrated the outer defenses
government officers joined civilians
in digging trenches and erecting
| barriers.


Meanwhile, government troops
organized counterattacks.
Assault Slackens Elsewhere.
The Communist assault slackened
on some other sections of the 90
mile stretch of the Peiping -Hankow
railroad as government reinforce
ments pushed southwark from
Chohsien, 40 miles south Of Peiping
and northward from Chihchia-
chualig.


Military observers speculated
whether the Communists retalia-
tory attack on Paoting and the vital
railroad had disrupted Gen. Chiang's
schedule for q quick death blow to
Kalgan. The government continued
its news blackout of the latter
operation.


Yesterdays attack on an Ameri-
can Marine ammunition dump near
Tangku raised speculation that Chi
lnese Communists Intentionally are
creating an incident to keep alive
their propaganda aimed at getting
the Marines out of China.

seeking ammunition was considered
unlikely. The Communists have
japanese weapons so American am

ican propaganda campaign now has

vinced any German was implicated

Marihuana is the drug of self de-

This is the conclusion of Public

the most exhaustive tests yet made
on the effects of this substance
smoked in cigarettes.


For the past 10 years, since mari
huana smoking was first recognized
as possible major drug evil because
Of the ease with which the material
could be obtained, the actual effects
have been subject of much dis
pute. Brutal murders and complete
mental and physical breakdowns
have been attributed to 1t. Some
scientists, on the other hand, have
claimed that its bad effects were
relatively small and that smokers
did not become physically addicted
to it, as in the case of opium prod
ucts.


Convicts Used in Tests.


The Public Health Service work
ers. headed by DR. Edwin c. Will
liams. used as subjects six Federal
prisoners, all previous marihuana
smokers They were allowed to
smoke as many drugged cigarettes
as they wanted for one month. Dur
ing this time, they were kept under
constant observation and given
constant battery of mental and
physical tests. All the men them
selves claimed the drug was harm
less. They insisted the cigarettes
increased their productive activity
interest in work and artistic ability
Among the subjects were musicians
and actors.


The men probably believed what
they said, but neither their behavior
nor the mental and physical meas
urements supported their claims.


During the first few days the
Public Health Service doctors re-
port, there were increased signs of
exhileration The subjects became
more laxative, were more active
and grinned and laughed great
deal. They generally became more
pleasant and easier to live with.


But after about the first week
most OF these Improvements disap-
pesred. Normal activity decreased.

BAY CITY, Mich, Mar. 9.-Swept
inshore by strong wind gusts, huge
ice foes moved glacier like on Lake
Huron beach resorts before dawn
today. crushing community of cot
tageS under weighty impact.


In the wake of the freak ice ram
page were 46 destroyed summer
homes on fashionable Killarney and
Ricomo Beaches. Eleven others
were damaged.


The gigantic foes were lifted onto
the shore by wind and water and
cracked into tumbling blocks that
ground cottages off their founda-
t1ons. Some piled as high as 40
feet.


Damage Over 100000.


No injuries were reported. Police
said one family only partially clad
was removed from danger by neigh
bors.


Damage was estimated at more
than 100000" by State police, who
said that figure might increase
when the area is surveyed.


Some residences were twisted
around on their foundations at
angles ranging up to As degrees. Liv-
ing rooms and porches were filled
with chunks of ice, an eyewitness
reported. In one area, only the
housetops were visible over the ice
and several cottages were surround
ed completely.


Rumble of Ice Gave Warming


Residents of the resort section, S
miles northwest of Bay City, re-
ceived warning of the ice movement
only when the crushing mass had
approached their homes, driven by
wind which had shifted around
2 am. to blow inshore from Saginaw
Bay.


One man was awakened when his
glassed-in porch collapsed under
the pressure. Another heard a grind
ing sound outside his window and
looked out to find the ice only a
foot away.


Although the area is primarily a
summer resort, many families oc-
cupied the cottages because of the
AioaoiiS Siioi ldSe.


Ice Piles 40 Feet High.


Piled as high as 10 feet along the
Worst-hit 300-yard stretch of the
beach, the cold mass stood immov-
able late today with only slight
evidence of melting. Police said an
other shift in the wind from Saginaw
Bay might force the ice beyond its
present $50 to ITS foot deep pene-
tration of the shore.


Roads leading to the scene were
blocked to all but property owners,
who started salvaging operations
after the wind died down and the ice
movement apparently had stopped =.


One cottage was upset by the foes
and burned when an oil stove caught
fire. Electric service was cut off to
the entire section.

HENDAYE, France, Mar. L.
France broke off all commercial
relations with Spain today by
closing the 300-mile long border
between the two countries in pro-
test against the continuance in
power of Generalissimo Fran
cisco Frances regime.


The official closure, effective at
midnight, was devoid of drama. As
the hour passed, frontier guards
patrolled both sides of the border
as usual. The weather was blustery
and rainy.


Actually, the frontier was closed
two hours before midnight when
the customs offices finished the
days work. The Paris Express ar
rived an hour late, but was per-
mitted to cross, carrying the last
regular travellers, mostly Belgian,
Portuguese and Spanish nationals.


The French action effectively
sewers all commercial intercourse
between the two countries, includ-
ing telegraph, postal, rail and road
communications. Foreign diplo-
mats. Red Cross and UNRRA work
ers are excepted from the ban on
travel, as are Portuguese, French
and Spanish nationals returning
home.


French Vice Consul Barred.


Spanish officials refused one
diplomat, the French vice consul at
Barcelona, permission to return to
his post. No reason was given.


The last person to try to cross
and fail-was young German at
tempting to return to his family in
Spain. He had entered France
illegally and had been apprehended.
French officials were trying to send
him back before the border closed,
but Spanish officials didn't want
him either.


The only commercial traffic which
will be permitted between the two
countries is food en- route to Por-
tugal or Switzerland, and UNRRA
supplies in transit through Spain.
Some concern was expressed here
that this might further cut the al
ready slim French food supply, since
France has been importing quanti-
ties of fruit and fish.


In Paris, the political bureau of
the French Communist party adopt
ed as a motto: Not one boat, not
one train, not one automobile, not
one bit of merchandise for Frances
Spain. Down with Franco. Long
live Republican Spain"

August by veterans, while the July
figure was 41.450. The report ex-
planned that in August the veterans

HARSON, India, Nov. 11-Twenty-
seven persons-men, women ana
children-died last night In new
outbreak of communal fury when a
mob burned the Moslem quarter OF
this hamlet of about 500 within l5
miles of India's capital, Delhi.


Arriving at sunrise, I counted nine
adults and IL children whose bodies
had been charred and one woman
and five children who either had
suffocated or had been strangled.
Most of the bodies lay outside the
ruins OF mud houses, apparently
where the people had been struck
down and covered with inflammables
which then had been set afire.


Villagers told the district magis-
trate and police superintendent the
mob attacked shortly after nightfall,
|storming the Moslem quarter, strik-
ing down the inhabitants and firing
houses and bodies. One man esti-
mated the assailants numbered
about 100. Police could find only
three living Moslem men among the
villagers rounded up for preliminary
investigation on the scene.
Thirteen houses were burned in
whole or in part. Some of them still
were smoldering when British cor
respondent and I arrived about an
hour ahead of the investigating au-
thorities.


Houses of the sweepers (untouch-
ables), in the center of the Moslem
area, and the Sweepers themselves,
India's lowest Hindu cast, were not
touched.


The savage Staying and burning
constituted the sixth outbreak of
Hindu Moslem disorders since last
Thursday in an area lying east of
Delhi, toward and beyond Meerut.


District Magistrate Shanker Pra-
lsad of Meerut told me at the scene
of last nights carnage that the OFF,
cial figure Of fatalities from the six
Outbreaks was 321,

train rounded a curve on the pre-
cipitious banks of Meacham Greek

His regal robes are growing duller now
And hang about his form with languid air;
The crown of ice is melting on his brow,
The path behind him now appears less bare
He swings his sceptre meeky pow'r gone,
And moves his feet with trepidation rare.
He looks with doubt upon the coming morn
In fear of finding Springs fair heralds there
A tinge of green, a feecy cloud, the sun,
a waking bud, to haste him on his way,
Who, glancing backward finds his work is done.
Where rugged, ice-bound fury once held sway
Green-crusted Spring exerts usurped power,
Our verdant monarchy thrives meath her hand;
Her court bedecked with every living 1owr
Emits its hue throughout the fruitful land.
One sad forsaken spot of wintry white
Has sought for shelter meath some shrub in vain;
Our Frigid Vagabond now takes to flight
But to return and rule with might again.


RUBY MAE STEVENSON

BY the Associated Press.


TOKYO, Jan. 24.-Premier Shide-
hara conferred with Gen. Macarthur
for more than an hour and half
today on undiscloSed matters.


Elsewhere the japanese cabinet
was reported agreed to leave the
status of the Emperor virtually un-
changed in proposed constitu-
| tional revision.


There was no announcement by
Gen, MacArthur's headquarters
concerning his meeting with the
aged nobleman who carries out his
directives.


Macarthur Views Sought.
However, Kyodo news agency said
Shidehara discussed the political
situation since the recent cabinet
shakeup in compliance with Allied
orders to rid the government of men
who helped plan and wage the
Pacific war.


The press also said the Premier
sought Gen. MacArthur's views on
number of urgent measures which
the government is said to be con-
tenplating. Among these possibly
are the forthcoming election, pro-
posed importation of food and other
basic commodities, economic reforms
and prosecution of Japanese war
criminal suspects.


Jill news agency quoted reliable
sources close to the cabinet as saying
the status of the Emperor remains
substantially unchanged except for
a slight revision in the phraseology
of Article Three in the cabinets
draft of the proposed constitutional
amendment. Jill said Article Three
reading the Emperor is sacred and
inviolable" has been changed to "the
Emperor is supreme and inviolable." !"


Sale of Girls Halted.


Gen. Macarthur earlier ended
centuries-old custom under which
japanese families sold their daugh-
ters into the slavery of prostitution.


Gen. Macarthur ordered the Japa-
nese government to obey that sec
ton of the Potsdam Declaration
which guarantees respect for the
fundamental human rights" Under
1t Japan must annul all laws author
izing licensed prostitution and null
lily all contracts committing any
woman to prostitution.


The japanese government recently
halted licensing of houses, but not
the law permitting the sale of girls.
In 1910 the government had made
a radical change which permitted
the sale of girls only by blood rela-
tives, eliminating sale by husbands
and sWeethearts


Gen. Macarthur also acted to cur
tail imitation in economically be-
wildered Japan with an order which
froze the governments huge debt to
the Bank of Japan. The debt was
ordered retired quickly and the
japanese were directed to submit
complete government borrowing pro-
gram for the remainder of the fiscal
year which ends April 30.

CHICAGO, Aug. 5.-The cure of
alcoholism has become official State
business in Connecticut.


Three other States, New Hamp-
shire, New Jersey and Alabama
have earmarked funds for treatment
OF alcoholics and IA cities through
out the country have established
committees for education on alco-
holism.


This was reported today by the
Council of State Governments which
said surveys showed there are 750.-
600 alcoholics in the Nation, in ad-
dition to 2,250,000 Chronic" exces-
sive drinkers.


Yale Plan Adopted.


The Connecticut Commission on
Alcoholism has taken over the Yale
plan clinics for treatment of alco-
holics and the council described this
move as "a major step toward
broader public sponsorship of efforts
to cope with the fact that one male
adult out of every II in the United
States is an alcoholic or chronic
excessive drinker."


Under the Connecticut program.
the Yale plan clinic and its Hart
ford clinic branch will serve as pat
terms for similar units in other large
cities in that State.


The clinical treatment provides
for counselling without institution
alizing those who come voluntarily
or are sent by relatives or the courts.


The clinics are stated by a psy-
chiatrist, general physician, lay
therapist and psychiatric social
worker, and cooperate with Alco-
holics Anonymous and with public
and private agencies.


One Half Cases Cured.


The Yale clinics reported that
drunkenness has been checked-and
sometimes cured-in so per cent of
the cases whose trea atment has pro-
gressed beyond the diagnostic stage,
during which the patient talks to
staff members about his background
and problems.


During the guidance period, which
may run several months, the patient
has several talks week with a psy-
chiatrist. The patient also may drop
in or telephone the clinic when a
special problem arises.


The State spends from $50 to 500
to treat each patient.


Cities with local committees for
education on alcoholism, the coun-
Gil said, are Austin, Dallas and Fort
Worth, Tex; Boston; Charleston,
w. Va; Daytona Beach; Des
Moines: Pittsburgh; Rochester. N.

Washington, D. c.; New York and

earthquake and severe tida.
waves ravaged more than $4,000
square miles of Southern Japan
today.


Incomplete figures listed 500 dead
612 injured and 43 missing; nearly
$4,000 homes destroyed, damaged OF
flooded, and 500 fishing vessels lost
Only one Allied casualty missing
British soldier-was reported.


Seismologists said the quake pos

Six tidal waves, erupted by the tenn

rushed over Wakayama Peninsula
and inflicted damage over 370-mile-
wide area from ShimodA, on the
Eastern Honshu coast, to Kochi, on
Shikoku's southern coast. Some of
the waves were 10 feet high.


Authorities said loss of life was
not far greater because the quake
epicenter was under water.

Tonight, thousands of Waka-
yamans fed into the hills, fearful
of repercussions. Tanaba was de-
serted, its $500 homeless refugees
having sought safety in the hills.


Residents of some other Waka-
yama towns likewise fled, carrying
their meager possessions.


Only fragmentary information was
available from the two areas that
appeared hardest hit-the southern
coast of Shikoku and Western
Wakayama, both isolated.


An early estimate that probably
1000 japanese were killed-based on
a report that 200 families at Kochi
were wiped out''-was disregarded
later as Army and Japanese sources
compiled their reports of known
casualties.

ern tip of Honshu-was reported
washed away by '7-foot waves.

afternoon.

The famous cities of Kyoto and
Nara, both former Japanese capitals

The United States Military Gov
ernment said Osaka has five days

Damage extended from atom

bill was "debunked." I submit that it
Is the authors of the teen-age draft
scheme who have been emasculated.

Chinese Communist party, through
its New China Daily News. today
admitted its charge that American
planes had strafed Communist lines
in Manchuria was a mistake.


The charge, the paper said, re-
suited from the use by the Chinese
National Government of non perma-
nent paint in covering the mark
ings of aircraft purchased from the
United States.


The statement followed the ex-
planation by Gen. George C. Mar
shall April %, in denying the Com
munist assertion two days earlier
that American planes had strafed
Communist lines and that one had
been shot down with an American
flyer in it.


Gen. Marshall investigated and
learned, he said, that the Amer
ican" flyer was a Chinese national
pilot dressed in flying suit pur-
chased from the United States.


Gen. Marshall recommended that
the National Government cover the
insignia of all purchased planes with
permanent reint coats.

Street Battle Investigated.


The 6,043 elected county officials
took their seats on rural councils
today.


Meanwhile. American troops
closed off the displaced persons
camp at Diessen with road blocks
manned by armored cars and gun
carrying jeeps after an election day
fight in which one German was
killed and II were wounded.


The fight occurred at Landsberg.
near the Diessen camp.


A. c. Glassgold of New York City,
UNRRA director at the Jewish dis
placed persons camp, said the trou-
BILE developed when two Jewish
guards at the camp mysteriously
disappeared Saturday night and the
rumor spread that they had been
kidnapped and killed by Germans.

was said six Jews had been ma
chine-gunned by German civilians.


Aroused, the 4,500 Jews in the
camp stormed into Landsberg and
began attacking German civilians,
many of whom were on their way
to the polls.


Fight RACES in Streets.


Knives flashed and clubs were
swung as the pitched fight ragged
through the streets between individ-
ual Germans and Jews. A bus was
halted, its occupants pulled out and
the bus burned.


American troops were rushed in,
but it was not until five hours after
the fighting started that order was
restored.


Two hundred additional soldiers
were on guard today and an uneasy
quiet hung over the town.


Eighteen Germans were sent to
the hospital and one died. No re-
ports have been received of any of
the Jews being injured.


Unofficial reports indicated that
the two missing guards had left the
camp voluntarily.

Hesse that the Communists won
their biggest vote, polling per cent
Of the total vote of 1896, $50 cast in
the state, which includes the indus
trial cities of Frankfurt, Wiesbaden
and Kassel.


Yesterdays elections were consid-
cred more significant in political
sense than last Januarys local
elections, in which more than 80
per cent of the eligible voters turned

porary housing was in addition to

veterans, undertaken by the Ma

ing Expediter Wilson Wyatt.

last December for the conversion

owned buildings. 1t was estimated
this money would be sufficient for
the 100000 temporary homes. But,
FPHA said today, increased costs
have necessitated cutting the target
figure to 10000 because no addi-
tional money was provided before
Congress adjourned.


About half of this number, the
FPHA said, have been converted
with Federal funds and moved to
educational institutions and munich
palities for veterans use. Cities and
schools have supplied the utilities
and have agreed to dispose of the
housing when it is no longer needed

turned over 21,478 housing units to
cities and 42,856 to schools to be
converted at their own expense.
The schools and cities own these
outright, but have agred to use
them only for temporary veterans
housing.


The surplus structures, including
barracks, Quonset huts and other
military buildings, either have been
converted for use where they were
built during the war or have been
moved and re-erected at new sites.

Ever since I have been collecting
stamps have thought that one of
their most interesting features has
been the scenes which they picture.
I have always enjoyed saving stamps
with portraits of animals and birds
and I have been surprised at the
number which have those pictures.


The African countries, Nyassa and
Liberia especially, have printed
many colorful stamps to commemo-
rate the strange animals which in
habit their lands. Birds have often
been used as designs for airmail
stamps. Even Germany issued
stamps for eight years commence
rating the famous horse races held
annually at Munich.


I have noticed that most of the
stamps depicting wild life are issued
by the countries they inhabit. Aus
tralia, land of strange animals, has
issued more animal stamps than
any other British dominion. Other
British dominions and certain South
American nations have released in
teresting sets-even commemorating
fish!


The United States, however, has
issued only one such stamp-the 30
cent buffalo of 1923. With all the
interesting wild life in our country,
we ought to have more stamps about
them in the future.

An Eastern railroad system announces
that it will put two reproductions of
famous paintings in each of the 213
new streamlined lightweight cars now
in construction. Cars will be grouped
in trains according to the type of art,
so that Hudson River school and con-
servative British masterpieces won't be
commingled with Picasso, Van Gogh,
Matisse, Renoir and Cezanne. The
road plans to distribute booklets de-
scribing the paintings and listing the
museums where the originals hang.


This is another move to bring art to
the public. and surely praiseworthy. But
at least one Western editor doubts that
any "oid master" hung in a car will
approach in interest the countless and
ever-changing pictures portrayed in
real life on trains. For instance, the
Des Moines Register lists the young
mother taking her first trip with her
first baby. The starry-eyed honey
incoming couple. Kids on vacation from
school. Christmas, Easter and Thanks
giving crowds. The peppery old gentle-
man who can't get the window open
And the endlessly patient and cheerful
porter, more indispensable than deco
rations, radios. reading lights or free
matches

TO the Editor OF The star:


There have been many editorials and
articles written about Miss Mabel
Boardman since her death last Sunday.
But not yet have I read anything
written by volunteer worker Of no
Importance.


Miss Boardman not only founded the
Volunteer Special Services. She was the
Volunteer Special Services. Through her
many years In the American Red Cross
she worked for and with the volunteers
and when the need arose she fought
for them


Only those who were privileged to
work with Miss Boardman can possibly
realize the tact, the wisdom, the heart
and the fairness that was hers. No
problem was so small to take to her,
no problem was too great for her to
solve.


Although her days were full from the
time she reached the office until she
left. she was never too busy to see
and to help any worker who felt the
need for advice and assistance.


Two years ago when Miss Boardman
resigned from active work in the Dis
trict Of Columbia Chapter a luncheon
was planned In her honor. Hundreds
and hundreds of applicants were un-
able to buy tickets. Indeed, it was said
that II every hotel and restaurant in the
city of Washington had been made
available for this luncheon still there
would not have been room enough for
all those who wished to attend.


The people who worked longest for
Miss Boardman were the people who
loved her best. And not only did she
make others happy. she was happy
herself.


What better epitaph could she have
than:


"Iil ask OF death no greater boon
than this:


That it shall be as wonderful as
life"? SUSA STANTON SNYDER.

CLEVELAND, May 18-Planes
and Coast Guard boats searched
Lake Erie today for two crewmen of
an Army medium transport which
crashed into the water last night
after four other members of the crew
had parachuted to safety.


The Coast Guard reported that the
source of flares reported seen a mile
or two out in the lake early this
morning had not been located by the
patrols which were sweeping over a
wide area. Early belief was that the
missing pair might have been adrift
in a rubber boat.


Four crew members resorted to
their parachutes when the plane
ran out of fuel after bad weather
prevented the pilot from landing at
Cleveland Airport. The four chutists
landed about a half-mile from the
lake shore.


1t was not known whether the
other two crewmen got out of the
plane. which was headed for the
lake when the order to jump was
given.


Army Air Base officials at Cleve-
land Airport refused to release the
names of crew members accounted
for or missing. The plane was from

ess Wednesday night, police dis

jewel fences"

gang had planned. the haul and the
supposition that the search was be-
ing concentrated In France:


/. There were reports that Scot
land Yard had sent several ace
operatives to Paris to work with the
Surete, French crime detection
headquarters, in the belief the rob-
bers followed the duke and duchess

goes back more than a thousand
years, ever since the first Moham-
medan invasion of the peninsula
through the rugged northwestern
passes from what is now Afghanis-
tan. During much of this millennium,
the Moslem conquerors have domi-
mated India. and today nearly 100,-
100000 out of its 100000 900 inhabi-
tants profess the faith of Islam. Yet
the Hindus, especially the upper
caste Brahmins, still regard the
Moslems as impious interlopers who
pollute the sacred soil of Hindustan,
while the Moslems, on their side,
regard the Hindus as equally impious
idolators with whom no true peace
Is possible.


This ancient grudge, envenomed
by mutual fanaticism, always sim
merS below the surface, ready to
burst forth into wild violence at the
slightest provocation. The current
Calcutta riots were not deliberately
melted by the leaders on either side.
The Moslem League had ordered
mass demonstrations against the
failure of the government to grant
parity with the dominated
Congress party in the formation of
the proposed interim native govern
ment. Those demonstrations were
planned to be peaceful. But as soon
as they got under way, fighting ap-
pears to have broken out spontane-
ously between the Moslems and
Hindus who had gathered in rival
crowds. And those clashes quickly
developed into savage struggles in
which quarter was neither asked nor
given, terrible atrocities being COM
mitted and even little children ruth
lessly slaughtered.


The essentially religious nature of
the clash is shown by the fact that
neither Europeans nor other minori-
ties have been molested. The only
minority to be involved are the
Sikhs, who share the Hindus' antag-
onism for Moslems and seem to have
pitched in on the Hindu side. Local
Moslem and Hindu leaders have
come out with joint appeals to their
coreligionists to stop the fighting,
but the situation appears to have
gotten out of hand, the combatants
being blinded and crazed with blood

The strategic considerations which
underlie Russian policy toward Iran
and Turkey are worth examining. They
are probably much more important
factors in Russian reasoning than the
chances Of finding oil in Northern Iran.


The Russian leaders are obsessed with
the idea Of security for Russian from
tiers. They are well aware that they
have very little long-range air power,
and very little naval power. They are
well aware that it is these two types
of powers which make up the bulk of
the fighting strength of the United
States and Great Britain-Which are
the only other nations possessing any
military resources worth immediate So
Wet consideration. They are likewise
well aware that these two types of pow
er are of long reach and great mobility.
Finally, the internal communications
of Russia are poor, and grow poorer
the farther one gets away from the
central area of Russian power. Around
the vast fringes of the Russian land
mass, there are good many places
where American and British sea and
air power could produce concentrations
of strength much more rapidly than
Russian land power could be concen-
trated to meet it. This fact makes the
Russians nervous about such parts of
their frontiers. The total inability of
the Germans and the Japanese to meet
and deal with unsupported amphibious
concentrations has not been lost on the
Russians. The answer which they seek

strategic areas in order to gain time for

BALTIMORE, July 1s.-The State
of Maryland has snapped its steam
er Dupont for the Coast Guard
Cutter Potomac, formerly Presi-
dent Roosevelt's yacht.


Gov. O'Conor announced the
exchange yesterday following con-
ference with Secretary of the
Treasury Snyder. The Dupont had
been loaned to the Coast Guard
in 1912 and had been extensively
reconditioned by that service.


The transfer was decided on since
restoring the Dupont to it's former
condition was considered impractical
Gov. O'Conor said.


Acquired in 1882, the Dupont
served as flagship of the Tidewater
Fisheries Enforcement Fleet along
with a second stamer which was
sold last year. The erstwhile Presi-
Dental yacht will replace both in
patrolling Maryland waters, the
governor said.

ments when the first gust of strong
wind followed rain and hail. The

night shopping rush.

Dairy specialists pointed out that

and with the advancing milk prices
making dairying more attractive to

adjust his business for maximum
returns. A greater fall production
should assist in this adjustment.


Specialists cited five reasons why
dalrymen will profit more by hav-
ing larger number of cows freshen
in the fall and winter. They are


l. Fall and winter freshenine
cows produce more milk and they
produce it more evenly throughout
the year than do spring-freshening
cows. In the spring. the fresh
pasture and favorable weather re-
stimulate the milk production oi

of their lactations.


Uniform Distribution.

portunity for greater net profit with
good COWS and dependable labor.

fresh COWS when they are naturally
at their highest levels of production


4. Calves from fall-freshening

time. Furthermore, when spring
comes, the calves should be de-

Unfortunately, when q herds pro-

1. Management: Establish we'll

Provide an environment that will

2. Keep only good producers and
feed them literally: Good breeding
and liberal feeding of top-quality
homegrown hay and silage in
winter and abundant pasturage

lower harbor yesterday

ment under the care of officers

read the decommissioning orders
and signaled the Idaho's colors
hauled down for the last time.


The 33000-ton battlewagon sailed
into eight naval engagements dur
ing the war and participated in ls
bombardments. Her guns fired $500
tons of shells, and she Travelled
190,775 miles.


Three times the Axis radios sank
her, but she actually was hit only
once. A bomb fell on her deck dur
ing the bombardment of Okinawa
on Easter morning, 1945.

be glad to 60 back to work tomorrow.

little subbosses, the political satraps
of organized labor who, for the first
time, have seen their names in the
papers, and who have by reason of their
unchallenged power, rule with iron
hand their subordinates. \

paper Neue Zeitung,

by Franz Neumann, chairman of the

followers to cast void ballots in Rus
sian zone elections.

printing them the German papers

ing the Allies.

American-held newspapers could

The reactions of the riding public
to the microphone-speaker units
installed experimentally this week

streetcar have been definitely
good" company officials said today.


The units, which are being tested
both for public reaction and me-
chanical defects, are used by drivers
to announce stops. transfers and ask
the public to move to the rear of
the car. please"


Previous experiments with speaker
systems on the vehicles had proved
unsuccessful due to "feedbacks,
squawks and grating noises COM
pany officials said. They added,
however, that the present equip
ment, with microphone small
enough to be attached to the collar
of the driver, was developed spe-
cially for the purpose.


The company expects to test the
units for several months before de-
Gliding whether to install them on all
cars and buses.

MANILA. July Is. - American
civilian employees of the United
States Army are complaining to
the Embassy and the Army that
living conditions are not as good
as they were promised when they
were recruited for overseas service.


George Claybaugh of Topeka,
Kans., engineer. who acted as
spokesman for the employees, said
they had been promised modern
homes, low mess costs, officers club
privileges and recreational facilities.


Instead, he said, they arrived
here to find husbands and wives
were forced to live apart in gloomy
barracks in a muddy area more
than 10 miles from Manila, that
there were no recreational or trans
port facilities, and no place where
husbands and wives could even
meet in off hours.


In addition. he said, the employees
had been told they would pay
Philippine income taxes, but found
they were subject to the higher
American taxes instead.


Army headquarters acknowledged
that housing was not vet ready,
but said facilities met the terms
of the contracts and they did not
know what promises recruiting
agents may have made in the
United States.

Senator Taft, Republican, OF Ohio
states the philosophy underlying
much of the labor legislation that
will be debated in the new Con-
gress.


THE general labor question" he
said in an interview, eis correcting
an unbalance of power.


Senator Taft, who may have more
to say about labor bills than any
other man in the Senate. said thai
formerly the employer had all the
power, but because of laws, court
decisions and administrative ac-
tions, it has shifted completely to
the labor side"


Union leaders angrily deny that
unions ever gained more bargain
ing power than corporations. Their
voices will be heard, but not so
strongly as before.


Several Possibilities Seen.


Labor law proposals fall roughly
into these groups:


/. RepaSsage of the Case bill,
which President Truman vetoed last
June.


2. Rewriting of the Wagner Act
of 1885, which unions call "labor's

The District should have a pro-
gram for the care of disabled per-
sons which could be model to the
rest of the country, a House SUBJ
committee reported today.
Like most States, the subcommit-
tee on Aid to the Physically Handi-
capped said, the District falls very
far short OF this excellence" in the
scope and efficiency of its present
program.


Except for veterans, the country's
handicapped citizens are not getting
a square deal from Federal, State
or local governments, the report
said.


The subcommittee told Congress
that the extent and type Of aid given
was inadequate. haphazard and un-
evenly diffused" The report added


The existing inadequacies have
placed great burden of bitterness,
pain, waste, ignorance, insecurity,
idleness, hopeIessness and death
upon the physically handicapped and
their families"


The subcommittee mentioned lack
of enough special schools for handi-
capped children, enough visiting
teachers for shut-in children; lack
of adequate artificial limbs and of
enough wheelchairs and other need
ed devices.


The Federal Government, said the
group, has granted aids in "a piece
meal and fractional manner"


AS a start in the right direction,
the subcommittee recommended an
agency headed by cabinet officer
to direct health, welfare, education
and social insurance plans.


Other recommendations were for
more intensive research into dis
abling diseases and into the care of
the victims of these maladies and
of accidents. Preventive measures
on big scale were suggested More
liberal provision for the blind and
others was urged.


The subcommittee, branch of
the House Labor Committee, is
headed by Representative Kelley,
Democrat, of PENNSYLVANIA.

The inmates of the District Home
for the Aged and Infirm at Blue
Plains had their first Christmas
party today with a huge tree and
hundreds of gayly-wrapped presents
stacked around it.


Three hundred of them sat row on
row in the dining room responding
enthusiastically to the entertain
ment.


The idea of Christmas party at
Blue Plains was that of Alice Lane,
who conducts woman's program
over Radio Station WWDC. Ben
Strouse, owner of the station, asked
Otto j. Cass, home superintendent,
what the inmates wanted as Christ
mas presents and was surprised at
the list. They wanted tooth paste
and tooth brushes, combs, cigarettes
and pipe tobacco. Those things can
not be bought for them on a food
budget of 80 cents a day-13 cents
a meal-Mr. Cass explained. The
radio people kept plugging the party
over the air, adding such suggestions
as flannel night gowns and pajamas


People have remembered the men
and women at Blue Plains at Christ
mas time. The Baptist Young
Peoples Federation sends present
to every inmate. Other religious
groups were interested and each
Christmas various groups of Gov
ernment employees at the Federal
Works Agency, the Veterans Admin
istration and other bureaus chose
Blue Plains for Yuletide charity. But
there never had been a Christmas
party there.


The spectators roared when Nor
man Reed, WWDC announcer,
dressed as Santa Claus, lost his pill
low-stuf1ing. They gave Mike Hun
nicutt hand on his White Christ
mas" solo. But it was the appear
ance of child entertainers that won
their hearts. The old men in front
roared and slapped their knees when
8-year-old Barbara Gantrell sang
"Doin' What Comes Naturally" and
two other children, Claire Taylor and
Mary Boyd, tap danced on table.

BALTIMORE, July 4.-The 27-
year-old battleship Idaho, veteran of
more days of combat than any other
prewar United States capital ship,
was quietly decommissioned in the
lower harbor yesterday.


Sealed from the sea and air by
coverings and protective compounds,
she will rest at her pier in retire.
ment under the care of officers
and 25 enlisted men.


A small crew lined the deck as the
skipper, Comdr. Robert w. Downes,
read the decommissioning orders
and signaled the Idahos colors
hauled down for the last time.


The 33,000-ton battlewagon sailed
into eight naval engagements dur
ing the war and participated in 1a
bombardments. Her guns fired $500
tons of shells, and she Travelled
190,775 miles.


Three times the Axis radios sank
her, but she actually was hit only
once. A bomb fell on her deck dur
ing the bombardment of Okinawa
on Easter morning, 1945.

The mother of missing West
Newton (Mass.) schoolgirl walked
into Gallinger Hospital at Q am.
today and identified an amnesia
victim there as her daughter, Con-
stance Ann Nordheim.


Hospital attendants said 15-year-
old Constance recognized her mother,
Mrs. Anna Nordheim, but was still
vague about such matters as how
she happened to be in Washington.


The girl, tentatively identified as
Constance Nordheim by papers in
her purse, was taken to Gallinger's
observation ward after she collapsed
Thursday night in drugstore at
Eleventh and G streets NV.


Mrs. Nordheim rushed here after
the Missing Persons Bureau notified
the Massachusetts, State police that
a girl believed to be Constance Nord-
helm was here. The State police
wired back that a girl of that name
had disappeared Tuesday.


Constance told attendants today
that her mother had visited her
during the night, but that she still
couldn't remember whether she had
a father, brothers and sisters.


She knows she came to Wash
ington by train, but she says she
doesn't remember how she came
to leave home or whether she
Travelled alone, hospital authorities
said.


Mrs. Nordheim was expected at the
hospital again today to help jog
her daughters memory. Gallinger
authorities said they had been told
that Constance collapsed on the
street near her home year ago
and suffered from amnesia for sew
eral days.

NANKING, Oct. 12.-Govern-
ment capture of Kalgan. which
the Chinese Communists made
their No. 1 military citadel,
prompted many observers to
conclude today that China's
peace talks were definitely
doomed.


Communist sources conceded the
loss of Kalgan was a severe blow.
They promised that the fall of the
city would unity all Communists
and make them fight the govern
ment armies harder than ever.


The Communists had insisted
they would not return to the peace
table until the government called
off it's drive on Kalgan, city of
even greater strategic value than
their political capital at Yenan.


Gen. Chou Refuses Comment.


Gen. Chou En-lai, who walked out
on peace talks in Nanking when the
government loosed its multiple drive
on Kalgan, refused at Shanghai to
comment on the fall of the fortress.


Previously he had told General
issimo Chang Kai-shek through in
termediaries that If the government
captured Kalgan, China would be
split wide open and the responsible
ity would lie with the government.


In addition to it's position on the
important East-West Peiping-Sui-
yuan railway, the city was a hub for
highways leading both to Siberia
through Outer Mongolia and the
Communicated zone Of Northern
Manchuria.


The Ministry of National Defense
announced that Kalgan was cap
tured yesterday, few hours after
word was flashed from the front that
the first of Gen. Flu Tso-yi's troops
drove into the city from the west.


The main Communist defenses lay
to the southeast and this entry by
Kalgan's back door may have taken
the garrison by surprise, although it
was known that Gen Fus columns
were approaching.


Fled to Escape Trap.


The apparent ease with which the
government army took Kalgan in
dicated, however, that the Com
munists had withdrawn to escape
entrapment, taking to the hills that
surround the city.


The Communists moved into Kali
gan in August, 1915, shortly after
Japan surrendered. The city be-
came the major link between Com
munist zones in Manchuria and
Inner Mongolia.


Communist dispatches from Lini,
capital of the Reds liberated area"
in Shantung Province, said Govern
ment warplanes made two bombing
and strafing attacks on the city
Wednesday. There was some dam
age, but no casualties. the dispatches
added.

the hot-lunch program. The num-

this year under the National School
Lunch Act.


DIR. Ockey estimated that $173,445

funds, plus another $35,949 for eat

Children unable to pay for the

charge.

TOKYO, Nov. 2.-Japanese polit-
ical, economic and publishing circles
stirred uneasily today over re-
ports that Gen. Macarthur ultra
nationalist purge order will be en-
forced strictly.


Rigid application of the directive
would shake Premier Yoshida's Con-
servative cabinet, dethrone many OF
Japan's top industrialists and pos
sibly change the complexion of a
majority of the nations newspapers.


Many top-ranking International
lists lost their Offices shortly after
the purge order was issued last
January. Then enforcement was
relaxed while the government strug-
gled with many economic and other
problems and passed a new con-
stitution.


Many Japanese predict that pro-
mitigation of the new constitution
tomorrow will signal a renewed
purge.


Publishing circles especially are
showing anxiety. The purge might
remove many men whom liberal
Japanese accuse of tanning the
flames Of war and drumming up a
wartime spirit.


The purge also might sweep from
ONCE many civic and rural omcials.

JERUSALEM, Sept. 3.-The
400-ton ship Four Freedoms,
crowded with 1000 Jews seeking
to enter Palestine Illegally, ar
rived at Haifa early today in
tow of a British destroyer which
intercepted her last night off
Tel Aviv:


The Jewish immigrants were
transferred to the transport Empire
Haywood today for the trip to
Cyprus. where they will be de-
tanned.


Interception of the ship was ac-
companied by a brief fight between
the immigrants and a naval board
ing party during which several
British sailors were injured, the
British government announced.


Shortly after the vessel dropped
anchor between two destroyers just
outside the Haifa breakwater naval
engineers set up barbed wire rum
ways on the, docks for processing
the immigrants. Barges swarmed
around the anchored craft.


Just before noon one Of the flank
ing destroyers left the immigrant
ship and wheeled into formation
with cruiser and two other destroy
ers deployed outside the breakwater.
Two planes circled overhead.


A series of depth charges doomed
across the bay for about Is minutes
and Haifa residents expressed be-
lief that the bombs were being
dropped ito discourage the ships
passengers from attempting to swim
ashore"


The ship was first sighted about
IS miles off Tel Aviv. but was not
interfered with until she entered
Palestine coastal waters.


Fighting developed when the
British destroyer ChilderS dis
patched boarding party to inspect
the vessel and the immigrants re-
sisted, the British government an
nounced. During the melee at least
a dozen of the immigrants leaped
over the side, apparently with the
intention of swimming to shore"
the announcement said.


1t did not disclose their fate or
whether any of the immigrants had
been injured in the fighting.
The vessel was the first to arrive
in Palestine waters with load of
illegal immigrants since the British
announced that all Jews attempting
to enter the Holy Land without
proper admission certificates would
be deported to Cyprus.


Palestine sources who could not
be identified said the ship probably
was the first of new group of YES
sells now en- route to Palestine.


1t was believed that the immi-
grants had hoped to effect a landing
somewhere near the all-Jewish city
of Tel Aviv, where some 300 Euro
pean refugees were successfully
smuggled ashore several weeks ago.

United States have quietly changed
a long cherished and traditional
concept. Since pioneer clearings
became settled farms, hallmark OF

years has been clean fence rows.
More than a century ago as the
Conestogas rolled westward they
carried the old saying with them:
"You can tell a good farmer by his
fences, woodpile and harness"


Today farmers have come to real
ize the validity of the lesson taught

the best agricultural areas OF the
Nation, where fences have been kept

been methodically moved each sum-
mer, the balance of nature has been
destroyed. The songbirds, pheasants,
snakes and small animals have dis
appeared. All kinds of grubs, in
sects and plant pests have increased.
For half century the annual bill
for poison sprays and chemical in
secticides has been steadily mount
ing. This years bill Is conserva.
lively estimated at more than $780,
000, 900.


Brushy areas along farm boupd-
ary lines mean sanctuaries for
essential wild Life. We are at long
last learning a lesson from the hus-
bandmen Of the Old World countries,

ANNAPOLIS, Md, May 11.-Allen
Walz had his revenge here today as
Wisconsin's statuesque crew out
stroked the class of green field in
winning the Eastern Association of
Rowing Colleges championship, the
years biggest affair of its kind. 1t
was the Badgers first crew title of
any description. The winning time
for the mile and three-quarters was
s:124s.


The laugh was on Walz a few short
years ago when the youthful blade
mentor, then at Manhattan, saw his
crew bow to a Miami (Fla) Univer-
sity eight with girl, Sally Stern,
powdering her nose in the coxswain's
seat. Crimson checked Walz, who
never pulled an oar, officially, until
after graduation from New York
University, quietly handed in his
resignation and left. 1t was huge
joke on him.


But the boys laughed on the other
side of their faces yesterday while
watching the Badger blades sweep

Never did the Walz workmen let
their beat fall below IS strokes a
minute and at the finish, with Navy
and Columbia challenging, they
were knocking better than 40 with

Richly Deserves Crown.


Wisconsin was the dark horse and

scant four lengths separated the first
five boats with Navy second, Colum-

NIT. and Harvard in that order,
the last never in the race.

slowly in the rowing start, trailing
Columbia, Princeton and Navy. But
scarcely a quarter mile from the
stake boats the Midwestern sweep
swingers were third, pushing their
needle like prov into the leaders.


Navy took over the lead at that
point, hitting steady 80 beat, with
Columbia second and Princeton
back in fourth. At the next call the
Middies still had the edge, but
Wisconsin was gulping water in
huge strokes and rapidly pulling
to the fore with the other positions
unchanged.


Badgers Turn on Heat.


With mile of the grind left, the
picture changed rapidly. Wiscon-
sin. apparently coasting along, be-
gan to row, and with Coxswain
Carlyle Fay knocking out 38, went
ahead of the parade. Navy was
next, Columbia third and Prince
ton fourth. Walt Krstich. Navy
stroke, kicked the beat to SO and
Holz responded with 40. Other
crews were straining like galley
slaves as the frail craft glided
through the final and telling quar-
ter-mile, but Wisconsin had more
than enough to beat them off, while
Navy and Columbia were good
enough to hold second and third.


Rutgers, finishing with the fren-
zied whirl of an egg-beater, got
up in time to clip Cornell by a
splinter, but the rest merely pad
died out the distance, thoroughly
beaten.


A strong cross-Wind, estimated at
80 knots when the Junior varsity
boats began their upstream race
and at 20 when the varsity's swept
into action, delayed the start of the
program and forced Referee Col.
Howard w. Robbins to decide on
rowing starts. One stake boat was
swamped while the jayvees were lin

anchor, precluding standing start
for the varsity pull.


Navy Gains Revenge.

too, for with Admiral Chester MINI

Columbia to atone for a setback
administered by the Lions two weeks
ago on the Harlem. Cornell, pre-
race favorite, never seriously threat
ened. dogging the leaders rudders
all the way. The Big Red, stroked
by Dick Randolph, tired near the
finish as Rutgers came on with
fighting finish to sneak into fourth
spot.


Several thousand spectators, some
in bleachers ashore opposite the
finishing buoys and others in small
boats following the crews, witnessed
the races, and saw Princeton sneak
home winner in the opening jay

Bogs are fascinating hunting

as full Of water as sponge. Walk

Actually, bogs are always in the
process of building up rich, fertile

matter gradually become almost
solid. 1t is vital that bogs in many
areas be left as a reservoir for

fred five rounds and charged with

only earnings subsequent to 1912

The thighs very often accumu-

balance. Bend both knees and touch

as though you were trying to lift

upward

arms extended out on the floor from

touch the left foot to the right
hand. Swing back to place. This
time swing the right leg over the
left and try to touch the left hand
with right foot Continue in a
smooth swing. allowing the hips
to roll and keeping the knee of
the leg which swings over, entirely
straight.

MOSCOW, July s tP).-A Tass
dispatch from Paris today said the
major problems at the foreign min
listers conference were solved when
agreements we're reached July 4 on
questions centering around the
peace treaty drafts.


The friends of peace will view
with satisfaction the results already
achieved at the Paris ministers con-
ference" the Tass correspondent
wrote. The question yet to be
solved concerning particularly the
Balkan treaties should not offer
special hardships, according to the
general opinion"


Reviewing the Paris conference
and the results obtained so far, the
writer said Foreign Minister v. M.
Molotov and the Soviet delegation
took firm stand from the start
against moves that placed what he
termed conflicting and half -digested
proposals before the peace treaty
conference.


The Tass writer said the United
States and Britain insisted stub
bornly on convening the peace con-
ference before completing their
main job of preparing peace treat
ies," but showed what he described
as even greater intractibility on
Italian reparations and the Italian
peace treaty until agreements were
finally reached.


Yuri Zhukov, commentator for
the newspaper Izvestia, also writing
from Paris today, said the British
were trying to build up Mediter-
ranean monopoly in communica-
tions by retaining control of Italian
cables that they seized during the
war.

appropriation bills.


American Red Cross measures

FRANKFURT, Jan. l9-Approx-
imately 100000 Germans will 60 to
the polls tomorrow in the United
States zone for their first free elec-
ton since Adolf Hitler seized
power 13 years ago.


The election, a local one, is for
the selection of town councils for
communities of less than 100000
population. There are 1000 such
communities in the American zone
but only about 1900 of them, all in
the northern province of Greater
Hesse, will vote tomorrow. The
others will ballot Sunday, January
27.


The voting will be watched closely
as an important experiment in the
military governments program of
reviving the processes of self-gov-
ernment among people who almost
have forgotten how to participate
IN the affairs of their own govern
ment. But neither German politi-
clans nor military government OFF,
cials expects the voting to disclose
much concerning Germanys politi-
cal trends, because of the local char
acter of the elections.


American occupation forces have
been instructed to keep hands off
the elections unless public disturb
ances arise which cannot be handled
by German police" The military
government wishes to give the Ger
mans the fullest opportunity to dem
onstrate their own capabilities


German politicians have protested,
and the military government has
admitted, that there have been eff
forts by known Nazis to dissuade
would-be voters. The political lead
ers, almost unanimously, also have
objected that the elections were
being held too soon to permit proper
Organization.

air transport.


Discussing his views during the
nrSt airborne demonstration of a
nylng post offlce-sorting mail in

outlined this general program:

trade areas. For example, trans

ida, New Orleans and the South

with the flying mail car" runs.

munity size would complete the air.

BALTIMORE. Oct. 25.-Duck

illegal in Maryland's small streams
this year despite an earlier regula-
ton permitting this form of hunting.


The regulation was rescinded yes
terday after a stormy public hearing
for hunters and marsh owners held
before the State Game and Inland
Fish Commission.


About 200 duck hunters, many
from the Eastern Shore and South
ern Maryland, were present for the
two-hour hearing. The commission
voted 81 to rescind the order per
mitting hunters to shoot wild water
fowl from handpropelled boats in
streams not over 100 yards wide.

July and amended later to prohibit
such shooting within 200 yards OF
an occupied duck blind. The hearing

Proponents of the ruling were
chiefly hunters with no regular

exhorbitant.

large duck shooting properties
members of private duck shooting
clubs and muskrat marsh propri-
etors, who said it would permit in
fringement of their property rights


The commission appointed a
three-man committee to examine
the present duck blind license law
to find ways to make it more equit-
able and to consider the problem
of providing more public wild water
fowl shooting areas. Named to the
committee were State Game Warden
Ernest H. Vaughn and A. Gordon
Fleet and j. D. Longfellow, members
of the Game and Inland Fish Com
mission.

RIO DE JANEIRO, Aug. 3l.-Riot-
ing which stemmed from Brazil's
economic crisis killed one person
and injured nearly 100 as mobs
moved through downtown streets
smashing store windows last night.


Sporadic attempts to renew the
demonstrations today were foiled
when merchants, after opening their
shops briefly, slammed steel shutters
across the store fronts. Police at the
same time were busy dispensing
crowds.


Police reported 200 registered Com
munists had been arrested. The au-
thorities prohibited the use of
Communist headquarters.


An extraordinary session of Con-
gress was being considered.


Plate glass from store fronts was
scattered throughout the business
section of the Brazilian capital. The
mobs, protesting against high living
costs, attacked movies, grocery
stores, music shops and even funeral
parlors.


Troops occupied strategic points
at midnight, but later returned to
barracks.


Federal Police Chief Pereira Lira
said in an official communique that
the riot in which groups of high
school students participated, was
inspired by more serious motives
than a mere student demonstration.
He did not elaborate, however.

The Democratic-Labor coalition, so
strong during the past II years. has
been badly shaken by the railroad-coal
labor crisis. Labor's counter offensive
against President Truman has been
sharp and serious. The Whitney out
burst, the hate Truman rallies, Sidney
Hillman's telegraphic offensive, the
attacks by Roosevelt stalwarts like
Messrs. Morgenthau and Ickes are all
signs of the weakening, if not the
breakup, of an alliance which always
has been opportunistic. These symptoms
may wear off because it is not probable
that these discontented people will move
into the Republican party. And Messrs.
Truman and Hannegan will pass out
plenty of olive branches But the present
uproar on the left certainly will carry
on into the 1916 election and seriously
affect its results.


Because of this break, opponents of
labor will stiffen their opposition. Con-
gressional candidates whose natural
inclination is to oppose close labor
Affiliations will be bolder. The use of
union money in congressional contests
will be more openly resented Congress-
men will vote more freely for measures
limiting the power of labor.


X X


But grave weaknesses in the CIO-PAC
effort to dominate elections will show
up sharply. These weaknesses were ap-
parent even before the late crisis. The
PAC has been unsuccessful in its con-
tests in Southern primaries. And even

OTTAWA, Mar. 13.-Two of the
four persons accused of participating
in the Russian-sponsored spy ring
in Canada were arraigned in court
again today to hear additional
charges against them.


The two were Mrs. Emma Woikin
cipher clerk in the Department OF
External Affairs, and Miss Kathleen
Mary Willsher, 40, assistant registrar
at the Office of the United Kingdom
High Commissioner to Canada.


The additional charges. under the
Official Secrets Acts were similar to
charges presented when the accused
first appeared in court two weeks
ago.


The new charges against Mrs
Woikin, bringing her total to six
are that she made confidential notes
useful to the Russians communicated
confidential documents to unauthor-
lied persons, used information for
benefit of the Russians and retained
confidential notes in her control.


The additional charges against
Miss Willsher were that she COM
municated unauthorized informa-
ton to unauthorized persons and
used information prejudicial to the
state.


The original charges against Mrs
Woikin and Miss Willsher charged
them with conspiring to make in
formation available to the Russians
and with having made the informa-
ton available.

When the first warmth of real
spring was mellow on the land, the
farm wife always decided it was
time to move to the summer kitchen.
The first room of the ell was the
beginning of a series that linked
the main house to the barn. In the
northeast there was good reason to
join house and barn together, for
many were the stormy, lashing days
between November and April.


Good housewives were eager to
get back to the summer kitchen
come spring. Then the room that
during the winter months served as
the heart of home could become Just
the living room and the dining room
combined. A farm wife knows that
when April begins the men folks are
busy with spring work. Moving day
was usually on Saturday, so lad
and his sisters could help. After the
chores were out of the way, break
fast over and dishes washed, the
whole family pitched in.


Father and the boy washed the
ceiling and the plastered walls. All
the winters accumulation of odds
and ends was moved into the wood
shed, toolroom or the section of the
ell where the two-seated democrat
was kept. Then the windows were
washed, the cupboards scrubbed out,
the back pantry cleaned and the
floor, with its wide boards, mopped
several times. Sisters cleaned and
polished the smaller range that
served from April to November.
Then came the moving of the tall
wooden cupboard that mother al
ways wanted near the table where
she did the mixing-a cupboard that
father built as special gift when
he brought his bride to the old home
farm. Somehow moving day was
always good fun-one of the tasks
that brought the whole family to-
gether. And as a man looks back
nearly half century it seems that
mother always had some special
mincemeat-fllled cookies or pieces
of her famous three-layer chocolate
cake ready about eleven o'clock,
when the work of moving to the
summer kitchen was over for an
other year. ~

NEW YORK, Nov. 9.-The ground
work for Big -Four talks on German
peace treaty late this month was be-
ing prepared tonight as hopes rose
that the long deadlocked Trieste dis
pute might be near a solution.


Preliminary attention to the Ger
man issue was given as the foreign
ministers took long weekend re-
cess after a weeks failure to make
any visible headway on peace treaties
for Germany's satellites.


Diplomatic sources believed that If
the Trieste dispute could be settled
within the next 10 days, the four
power ministers would be able ITO
tackle the German peace problem
earlier than had been expected.


Secretary of State Byrnes received
British Foreign Secretary Bevin in
his suite at the Waldorf-Astoria this
morning for almost an hour, but the
subject or subjects of their converse
ton were a closely guarded secret.


Diplomats, however, speculated
that the two may have discussed
the explosive Palestine issue. Mr..
Byrnes disclosed last week that
President Truman had turned this
issue over to him for future
handling.


In view of developments on the
Trieste dispute within the past "a
hours, some conference sources con-
sidered it likely that this was also
discussed.


i. Top Western diplomats predicted
that the Big Four would readily
scrap their whole elaborate plan for
internationalizing Trieste If Italy
and Yugoslavia could produce a
new formula for settling their bit
ter dispute over that city among
themselves.


There were increasing indications
that the Italians and Yugoslavs may
be attempting to reach a compro-
mise that would be acceptable to
the four-power Foreign Ministers.


Meanwhile, the Foreign Ministers
prepared to resume sessions Monday
in their skyscraper chamber coun-
Gil, tackling issues of disagreement
in the treaties for Romania, Hun
gary and Bulgaria. The Foreign
Ministers temporarily passed over
the Trieste issue this week when
they were unable to reach a solution

While searching for ice and
weather data, two naval patrol
planes flew to within $50 nautical
miles of the North Pole, the Navy
announced last night.


The planes, Martin Mariners, car
ried out their expedition with only
such special equipment as an cleo
trio gyro-compass, extra rations,
survival gear and winter fuels.


One plane flew between Green
land and the Canadian Arctic to the
Polar Sea. and then along the north
coast of the northernmost known
land in the world Another flight
passed over Cape Columbia, from
which Rear Admiral Robert E.
Peary set out for the Pole in 1909,
and then went over the Arctic
Ocean.


The planes, part of a combined
surface ship and aerial expedition
in the search of weather data. took
off from Thule, on the northwest
coast of Greenland. declared by the
Navy to be the northernmost point
that any large ship has ever reached
at this time of the year The yes
sells in the expedition are the Navy
Auxiliary Icebreaker Whitewood,
the, Coast Guard ce-Breaker-Cu
ter North, Wind and the Navy Sea-
plane Tender Norton Sound


The expedition, it was asserted,
did not sight the "Once dreaded
Middle Pack" which kept the area
icebound for many years during the
summer


While numerous iceberes were en-
countered by the ships, it was said
that the current summer appears
TO have been unusually good for
navigation in these waters. The area
covered to date was said to have
been practically free of ice packs.
Advance reconnaissance by the
Whitewood has indicated that the
southern limit of the pack ice now
lies in Kane Basin. and this Is said
to be further north than where it
is usually found.


But while cruising in this bleak
area. sunspots created some dis
turbance when they isolated the
ships of the expedition from radio
contact with the outside world for
more than a week. However, the in
cident was said to have been favor
able to the studies being made by
John Graham and John Barghau-

IN CITY after city the clang-
clang of the trolley bell is be-
ing drowned out by the honk-


honk of the bus horn.


Here in Washington-with its
mass transportation headaches-the
trolley is making last stand in
the form of the supertrolley We see
scooting almost noiselessly along
our streets every day. Styled the
Pee presidents Conference Com
mittee) car, this streamliner of ur-
ban rails is also being used in sew
eral other American cities.


A far cry from the old open sided
summer trolley or the winter cars
of yesterday which were equipped
with pot-bellied stoves frequently
fired by the passengers, the PEG
cars are the last word in modern
streamlining. They boast rubber
cushioned wheels, smooth starting
and stopping, quiet operation and
electrics braking. Cars like these,
transit experts believe, may con-
tinue to be used on major transit
routes in some large cities.


The buses may not have the per-
sonality of the old streetcars, but
they get the passengers where
they're going in better style.


Many cities already have made
a complete changeover from troll
leys to buses-among them Houston,
San Antonio, Syracuse, Fort Worth,
Jacksonville, Miami, Nashville, Hart
ford and Grand Rapids.


The trend began before the war.
Thomas E. Willier, transportation
engineer, reports that in 1884 there
were $4,000 streetcars and only 49,
TOO city buses in the country. Ten
years later the proportion had just
about reversed itself. with $1,000
streetcars and $4,000 city buses. Sew
eral hundred buses will be added to
that score next year in New York
alone, when the Third Avenue
Transit Co. hopes to replace all its
trolleys along five main thorough
fares, including Broadway and
Forty-second street.

VIENNA, Mar. 80. - A source
close to the Austrian government
said tonight Russian Army leaders
had withdrawn their demand for
l25, 900 acres Of Austrian farmland.
but had made fresh claim for
about 10000 acres.


This source said it was likely
that the withdrawal of the first
claim came as result of the dis
cussions at the Atlantic City
UNRRA Council meeting, but that
the new bid is for what the Rus
slams insist is German property
and thus Russia's under the terms
of the Potsdam agreement.


The new farms which the Rus
slams claim were owned largely by
Austrian Jews before 1888 and were
taken over by the Germans after
Anschluss. The farms include some
of Austria's most fertile acreages of
wheat and sugar beet country, the
informant said.


German holdings in Austria be-
fore the Anschluss were small. The
Russians, however. are interpreting
the Potsdam agreement to mean
that any property taken by the
Germans and held after Anschluss
until the end Of the war would be
subject to seizure for reparations,
the informant said The other
Allies take the position that prop
erty forcibly appropriated by the
Germans cannot be considered as
German property.


The question of land requisition-
ing was raised at the UNRRA meet
ing in Atlantic City this week, and
it was decided to withhold aid from
countries where all indigenous re-
sources were not being used Ap-
parently, the informant said the
Russians feel the appropriate of
the 10000 German" acres will
meet that objection.

Reversing a previous stand, the
House Military Affairs Committee
today approved legislation giving
enlisted service personnel the same
terminal pay rights that officers now
have.


The legislation would allow
maximum OF 120 days pay to Army
and Navy enlisted men at the time of
their discharge, provided they have
accrued the unused furlough time
when they are mustered out.


1t provides for the computation
of furlough pay at the rate of two
and one-half days for each month
of service. If man received actual
time off, he would not receive the
fwlough pay.


The committee earlier had shelved
the legislation after the Budget Bu-
reau said it would cost several billion
dollars and would pose "operational
problems of the most difficult solu-
tion."


The committee bill makes the
legislation retroactive to all enlisted
personnel who have served since the
draft law was enacted.

Bunker Hill last summer, but he's a
skipper without ship.


The Government has it-seized
September II by the Coast Guard,

decision holding it was not used in
the coastwise trading for which it
was licensed.

Yesterday exonerated Stralla and
three associates, George Garvin,
Elmer Perry and Ernie Judd, who

violate California gambling laws and

ordinances.

without jurisdiction over gambling

no Federal laws prohibiting it,
either.

bic Russian economic and political

of local Communist parties, whose
present party line is denunciation of
Yankee imperialism" and hostility
to the United States in every way.

Galapagos Islands, which lie far out

farther from the Panama Canal,
